en: *The Sūtra on the Non-retrogressive Wheel of Dharma*, Scroll One.
Recorded by Sengyou as one of the "Different Scriptures" from the region of Liang under Master An;
listed as the second translation in the *Beiliang Lu*.
1. Introduction: Chapter One. Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, together with a great assembly of twelve hundred and fifty bhikṣus, as well as an immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable number of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
At that time, after midnight, the World-Honored One entered the Samādhi of Vast Radiance Illuminating the Three Realms;
at that same time, after midnight, the Dharma Prince Mañjuśrī entered the Samādhi of Great Radiance Illumination;
and the Bodhisattva Maitreya, after midnight, also entered the Samādhi of the Universal Torch.

At that time, the World-Honored One arose from samādhi and, after midnight had passed, went out of his chamber together with Śāriputra and proceeded to the dwelling place of the Dharma Prince Mañjuśrī.

At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra saw that the rooms of the Dharma Prince Mañjuśrī and those of the World-Honored One were filled on all sides with lotus ponds. Within these ponds, immeasurable varieties of lotus flowers were spread across the water; each of these lotuses emitted radiance that illuminated the Jetavana Grove and the city of Śrāvastī, even extending to light up the entire trichiliocosm.
The great sound of the Dharma resounded throughout all worlds in the ten directions, where Bodhisattvas from various realms consulted one another, posing questions and engaging in discourse.
When the Venerable Śāriputra had entered the room, he saw Mañjuśrī in silent meditative concentration; standing before him, the Venerable Śāriputra then snapped his fingers and cleared his throat.
At that moment, the World-Honored One, Śāriputra, and the others beheld the supernatural transformations of the Dharma Prince Mañjuśrī, each seeing his own body within the great ocean.

At that time, Śāriputra was inside Mañjuśrī’s chamber and could not get out; he wished to leap into the void but could not move, nor did he know from where he had come, much less how he could depart by means of supernatural powers.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra sat with his legs crossed in the full lotus posture when he suddenly saw Mañjuśrī before him, sitting upright and composed.

Through the power of Mañjuśrī’s supernatural faculties, without leaving his original location, he caused Śāriputra to see Mañjuśrī in a world beyond worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, named Avivartika-saṃvāda-ghoṣa;
there dwelt a Buddha named Supratiṣṭhita-prabhāsa-vikāśana, currently existing in the world, surrounded by immeasurable billions of bodhisattvas.

He saw that from every pore of that Buddha’s body, lotus flowers emerged; each flower’s radiance illuminated the entire trichiliocosm. Each flower had a thousand petals, with stems of deep-blue lapis lazuli, filaments of agate, and pedestals made of various jewels.

Upon these flower pedestals, he saw bodhisattvas sitting cross-legged. Those bodhisattvas all dwelt in the stage of non-retrogression (*avaivartika*) and were destined to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. They had achieved great patience (*mahākṣānti*) regarding the gateways of dhāraṇī, adorned themselves with the thirty-two marks, and their bodies were of a color like pure gold, most subtle and supreme.

At that time, from the navel of the Buddha Well-Established Radiant Blossom-Expansion, there emerged a great lotus flower. Its colors were manifold and its petals immeasurable; it had a stem of deep blue lapis lazuli, petals of diamond, filaments of Indra-blue beryl, and a pericarp of dragon-firm sandalwood king, which could not be defiled by the dust or water of the world.

Śāriputra saw that this lotus pedestal was empty and devoid of anything, yet Mañjuśrī entered it and sat down; together with the lotus pedestal, they ascended as far as the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*). Mañjuśrī circumambulated the Buddha three times, joined his palms with single-minded devotion, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and sat cross-legged within the lotus pedestal, maintaining right mindfulness directed toward the Buddha.
At that time, the Tathāgata Supratiṣṭhitaprabhāvikasita asked Mañjuśrī,
“From which direction have you come to this place?
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
We have come from the Sahā world to this land.

In that Buddha-land there were two bodhisattvas, one named Good Sound (Svarasena) and the other named Good Voice (Ghoṣasena). These two bodhisattva-mahāsattvas had both already attained the stage of non-retrogression (avaivartika) and were certain to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. Emerging together from the lotus pedestals, they adjusted their robes, knelt with their right knees on the ground, joined their palms with single-minded devotion, and each addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How far is the Sahā world from here?
At that time, the Buddha Śubhavyūhaprabhāvikasita answered the two bodhisattvas, saying:
“Beyond worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges from this Buddha-field lies the Sahā world, and from there Mañjuśrī has come.
At that time, the Bodhisattvas Śobhanasvara and Śobhanaghoṣa both addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!...”
"In that world, what is the name of the Buddha?
I now wish to know this.
At that time, the Buddha Well-Abiding Radiant Flower-Blossom immediately replied:
"In the Sahā world, there is a Buddha, a Tathāgata, an Arhat, a Samyaksaṃbuddha, named Śākyamuni, who currently dwells in the world."
These two bodhisattvas asked again,
"What Dharma does Śākyamuni Buddha preach? That Buddha replied:
"I teach the Dharma of the Three Vehicles.
Thereupon, that bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"What are called the Three Vehicles?"
The Buddha said:
"What are called the Śrāvaka-yāna, the Pratyekabuddha-yāna, and the Buddha-yāna—Śākyamuni Buddha constantly teaches these three vehicles of the Dharma."
Then that bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
For what reason do the teachings of the Buddhas differ?”
The Buddha said,
"The teachings expounded by all Buddhas are entirely equal.
Those bodhisattvas then addressed the Buddha again, saying:
“What is meant by ‘equality’?
The Buddha said:
“The non-retrogressive wheel of Dharma is taught equally by all Buddhas.”
Then that bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One,
for what reason does Śākyamuni Buddha preach the Dharma of the three vehicles?"
The Buddha said:

"The minds of sentient beings in the Sahā world are for the most part inferior; if I were to preach the One Vehicle, they would not be able to understand it. Therefore, Śākyamuni Buddha, through skillful means, has brought forth all sentient beings from the five turbidities and, by differentiating and preaching the Three Vehicles, guides them so that they may enter the One Vehicle."
At that time, the two bodhisattvas addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Is the Dharma taught by Śākyamuni Buddha the most difficult to expound?”
The Buddha said,
"The preaching of the Dharma by Śākyamuni Buddha is truly most difficult.
The Bodhisattvas Good Sound and Good Voice addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
We have now gained a great and beneficial profit, for we were not born in such an inferior and evil land.
At that time, the Buddha replied to the two bodhisattvas, saying:
"Do not speak such words; you should quickly abandon them.
The Bodhisattvas Shan-yin and Shan-sheng addressed the Buddha again, saying, "World-Honored One!"
For what reason should we abandon these words?
In that evil age, it will be difficult to preach this Dharma; for this reason, we do not feel joy or delight now.
The Buddha said:

"To cultivate various roots of goodness for twenty billion nayutas of kalpas in this world is not equal to being in accord with the Prajñāpāramitās for the duration of a single meal in the Sahā world, causing a single sentient being to take refuge in the Triple Gem, uphold the five precepts, distance themselves from the minds of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, and resolve to attain the unsurpassed mind of bodhi."

It is far more difficult than that which involves twenty billion nayutas; how much more so for one who is able to encourage others to leave the household life, praise its merits, and extensively preach the Dharma so that they may transcend the three realms, thereby attaining their own benefit through such instruction, cultivating wholesome dharmas, and entering into various meditative concentrations.
"Why is this? Because these sentient beings are for the most part turbid and disordered by afflictions.
These two bodhisattvas again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Why is it that in that world, sentient beings are for the most part turbid and disordered by afflictions?
The Buddha said:

"If I were to describe to you for the rest of my life the defilements and disturbances of the sentient beings in this Sahā world—their greed, anger, and ignorance, as well as their immeasurable evil and unwholesome dharmas—I could not finish; only a Buddha can fully know the good and evil of karmic retribution."
At that time, those bodhisattvas, including Shan-yin and Shan-sheng, all together exclaimed in praise:
"This is truly Śākyamuni Buddha!
This is truly the Lion of the Śākyas!"

"He is truly the Sage of the Śākyas! Thus he offered these three kinds of praise: "Excellent is your teaching of the Dharma; excellent is your understanding of the thoughts of others. You have also extensively explained all unwholesome dharmas—greed, hatred, delusion, and false views, as well as immeasurable evils—and skillfully taught the paths to the good realms, the way of the śrāvakas, and the path of the pratyekabuddhas, all of which lead back to the Buddha, to the accomplishment of the Buddha’s wisdom, the foremost purity. One should resolve for bodhicitta, accord with liberation, and enter the Buddha’s wisdom."
For the sake of all sentient beings, they bring their roots of goodness to maturity with minds free from defilement.

Those bodhisattvas all together take up lotus flowers made of the seven treasures in various colors, each possessing hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of petals. They are like vajra-treasure repositories, with stalks of celestial deep-blue lapis lazuli, pedestals of dragon-firm sandalwood, and stems of manifold jewels, remaining unstained by dust or water.

Known by visual consciousness, these flowers are subtle and exquisite; they revolve spontaneously in the void and cannot be grasped. They arise from karmic retribution like shadows or illusions, and they also arise from liberation and various samādhis.

Having taken them up into the air, they scattered them from afar over Śākyamuni Buddha of the Sahā world. They held various flower garlands and flower canopies made entirely of diverse jewels, as well as jewel clouds, jewel canopies, and canopies of variegated silken fabrics, powdered incense, and ointment incense in immeasurable colors. Having thus made offerings to Śākyamuni Buddha, they prostrated themselves with their five limbs touching the ground before the Buddha and all spoke these words: “Namo Śākyamuni Buddha!”

In this Sahā world, the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas adorn the Great Vehicle with tireless diligence, cultivating all manner of meritorious virtues, and are fully capable of upholding all the true dharmas of the Buddhas of the past, future, and present. Desiring to deliver suffering sentient beings, they act as great illuminators abiding in the One Vehicle. We wish to go and see Śākyamuni Buddha, as well as the assembly of great bodhisattva-mahāsattvas of the Sahā world, who adorn themselves with great adornments in order to succeed to the lineage of the Buddhas so that it shall never be severed.

When the Tathāgata Well-Established Radiant Blossom-Flower heard these words of the bodhisattvas, he observed their minds and again spoke further of the merits of the Buddhas to instruct, benefit, and gladden them.

He addressed the bodhisattvas, saying: "You should follow and learn the path originally traversed by Śākyamuni Buddha. Generate a heart of great compassion and a heart of benefit toward all sentient beings; do not give rise to alarm, fear, or slander regarding the profound dharmas, but instead give rise to the signless (animitta). Fulfill your roots of goodness without seeking karmic retribution. Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who act thus shall all go to the land of Śākyamuni Buddha; through the power of their original vows, they shall be born there together with him, upholding the True Dharma and conforming to what the Buddhas originally practiced and learned. You may go and see him."
Those two bodhisattvas spoke thus:
"We shall go there by means of the Buddha's spiritual power, as well as the power of all past and future Buddhas."
The Tathāgata Well-Established Radiant Blossom-Openness addressed the Bodhisattvas Fine Sound and Fine Voice and the others:
"You should now go together with Mañjuśrī to the Sahā world."
He also said to Mañjuśrī,
"Go together with these two bodhisattvas to that place.
Then the two bodhisattvas said to Mañjuśrī:
“We wish to see Śākyamuni Buddha and the entire assembly of bodhisattvas; we shall be able to see that Buddha by relying on your supernatural power.
Mañjuśrī said to the two bodhisattvas, “Noble sons!...”

You should first pay homage to that Buddha, and you should also draw near to, make offerings to, and revere countless Buddhas; all this for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings throughout the worlds of the ten directions, for the purpose of increasing the Bodhi of the Buddhas, and also for the sake of accomplishing the wisdom of the Buddhas.
Those two bodhisattvas, acting according to his instructions, spoke these words:

“We, too, shall follow and make offerings to all the Buddhas, Tathāgatas; we shall draw near to them, prostrate before them, honor them, and praise them. We shall train ourselves like Mañjuśrī, desiring to bring benefit to all sentient beings.”

At that time, Mañjuśrī paid homage to the Tathāgata Well-Abiding Radiant Flower-Blossom, circumambulated the Buddha three times, and with reverence and respect, together with the various bodhisattvas and Śāriputra, proceeded to that place. Having arrived, he listened to the Dharma and received the Buddha’s instruction to contemplate the Tathāgata with focused attention. He made offerings by scattering flowers—incense powder, ointments, silk canopies, banners, and streamers of the highest purity—all of which were sustained by the spiritual power of the Buddhas of the past. With firm mindfulness and wisdom, he made universal offerings to the Triple Gem of the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṃgha for the sake of bringing all sentient beings to liberation.

In the time it takes for a strong man to bend and extend his arm, he suddenly appeared before as many Buddhas as there are sands in the Ganges in the eastern direction; in the presence of those Buddhas, he immediately exhorted them to extensively proclaim the pure wheel of Dharma of non-retrogression.

In these buddha-fields there are no women, nor even the names of the two vehicles—the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas—and they are no different from the buddha-field of the Buddha Well-Abiding Radiant Flower-Blossom, being adorned solely by great bodhisattvas throughout all the worlds.

From the pores and navels of all these bodhisattvas, lotus flowers emerged; within each lotus calyx there was a bodhisattva, and upon every single lotus calyx was a Mañjuśrī, all manifesting such supernatural transformations to make offerings to the Buddhas.

In the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, above, and below—even throughout the worlds of the ten directions—there were Mañjuśrī Bodhisattvas everywhere, all preaching the Dharma-wheel of non-retrogression. From each of these, two bodhisattvas emerged from within lotus pedestals and asked the Buddha:
"In that Sahā world, why is it called 'preaching the Dharma of the Three Vehicles'?"
They all desired to follow Mañjuśrī to see Śākyamuni Buddha.
At that time, the Dharma Prince Mañjuśrī comforted the bodhisattvas throughout the worlds of the ten directions, saying:
"I shall go together with you all to that Sahā world."
Upon arriving in Jambudvīpa, it was nearly dawn.

At that time, Ānanda, while the sky was not yet light, saw a radiance through the keyhole of the gate. He immediately rose and went outside, where he beheld a great light illuminating the entire Jetavana. Pure water, clear and limpid, filled the ponds to the brim; it was profound, mirror-like, and transparent, free from all dust and impurities, such that the groves, trees, and monasteries were no longer visible.
Having seen this, Ānanda immediately said:
"By what cause and condition has such a sign suddenly appeared?
Reflecting upon it, I am certain that this auspicious omen portends the preaching of the Great Dharma."

At that time, Ānanda entered the water; his feet did not sink, and the water did not cling to his body. With a joyful heart, he went to where the Buddha was staying. There were ten thousand lotuses emitting great music, and all the lotuses were seen to radiate light. This light shone everywhere throughout the Jeta Grove monastery, the city of Śrāvastī, and within Jambudvīpa, illuminating the entire trichiliocosm so brightly that it was like the light of day.
Ānanda leaped for joy and was filled with great rapture; he knelt on his right knee, joined his palms in reverence, and focused his mind single-pointedly upon the Buddha.
At that moment, the light of dawn appeared, and as the sun was about to rise, he saw ten thousand lotuses. Among them, one lotus stood out most preeminently within the Jeta Grove.

The Venerable Ānanda conceived this thought: "Today the World-Honored One must surely preach the Dharma; I shall spread out a seat to await the Tathāgata, for there are such signs of the preaching of the Dharma."
He immediately prepared a lion throne for the Buddha, and in a single instant, within a mere moment, the Buddha was seated.

At that time, the great earth shook in six ways; likewise, throughout the worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in the ten directions, it also shook in this same sixfold manner. The great trichiliocosm was strewn with celestial flowers—kumuda, puṇḍarīka, and utpala—and various fruit-bearing and flowering trees appeared spontaneously.
At that time, all the bhikṣus wished to go out, but seeing the great flood, their hearts were struck with alarm and fear, and none dared to leave.

They saw that the monastic quarters of the Jeta Grove were filled with the water of the pond, which was pure and free of defilement; all the trees, the monastic dwellings, the halls, and the gardens had vanished, and they saw only a radiance that shone everywhere without exception.
The bhikṣus all spoke these words together:
"This present auspicious sign must signify that the Great Dharma will be preached.

At that time, the World-Honored One arose from meditative concentration and sat down with serene composure. All Buddhas of the worlds in the ten directions emitted a great radiance, consisting of various jeweled nets of hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of countless colors, which could be perceived by the visual consciousness but could not be grasped.

Mañjuśrī, together with great Bodhisattvas from Buddha-worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in the ten directions, desiring to benefit immeasurable sentient beings, prostrated to, made offerings to, honored, respected, and praised each and every Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha. Accompanied by such Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas, his supernormal transformations were inconceivable; wishing to cause sentient beings to have faith in the Buddha-dharma so that they might be taught and benefited, he ensured that all could hear and see him according to their needs, skillfully preaching for them so that they all attained understanding and awakening.

At that time, Mañjuśrī knew that Śākyamuni Buddha had taken his seat; the entire great earth shook in six ways, and bodhisattvas emerged from the ground—numbering one asaṃkhyeya, a hundred asaṃkhyeyas, and even up to hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of asaṃkhyeyas—all gathered together and circumambulated the Buddha a hundred thousand times.

Furthermore, they took countless lotus flowers of various colors, with immeasurable and inconceivable petals, and scattered them over the Buddha. These were able to cause sentient beings to focus their minds single-mindedly and aspire toward supreme wisdom. The scattered flowers completely covered the trichiliocosm. There were also the fragrances of dragon-firm sandalwood and various other incenses—namely, the perfumes of the perfections of morality, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, wisdom, skillful means, and supernormal powers, all of which are the scents of the aids to the path that are free from conceptualization—as well as various other exquisite sandalwood and miscellaneous fragrances. All these were sustained by the supernormal powers of the Buddhas of the ten directions, and were used to make offerings to Śākyamuni Buddha.

At that time, Mañjuśrī, desiring to make offerings to all the Tathāgatas, together with a multitude of bodhisattvas, adorned a wondrous stūpa. He brought various maṇi eight-faceted jewels, as well as many jewel trees, silk canopies, banners, and pennants, and covered its summit with a lattice-work of assorted precious gems.

Furthermore, monasteries were constructed from *maṇi* jewels, with gates, screens, doors, and windows adorned in various ways. Ponds, springs, canals, and great rivers were covered with water lilies—*utpala*, *kumuda*, and *puṇḍarīka*—as well as lotuses made of various jewels. The water was always filled to the brim with the eight meritorious qualities (*aṣṭāṅga-guṇodaka*), and birds of diverse species gathered there to roam. Celestial jewel-trees appeared at will; these all served to deliver sentient beings and bring them liberation, causing them to resolve upon *bodhicitta* for the cultivation of Buddha-wisdom. All of this was the inconceivable miraculous transformation of Mañjuśrī, achieved through the power of the Buddha’s spiritual authority and the power of his vows, as well as the power of Śākyamuni Buddha’s original practices and vows.

Mañjuśrī performed these transformations because he desired to bring sentient beings to maturity and subdue them; with an inconceivable mind, seeing the inconceivable, he donned the great armor and entered the realm of the sages.

At that time, Mañjuśrī, together with the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, adorned all the wish-fulfilling flower trees and approached the Buddha. Whenever those bodhisattvas wished to sit, Mañjuśrī would first manifest a sign; in an instant, formless lotuses emerged from his pores, their stalks being of various kinds in immeasurable hundreds of thousands of colors, their petals numbering in the countless and inconceivable, with nets of light formed by diamond-treasures, stamens of celestial deep-blue lapis lazuli, and pedestals of dragon-hard sandalwood, wherein were bodhisattvas sitting cross-legged.

At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha emitted light from the center of his navel, which universally illuminated the dark and obscure places of the six realms of existence. These billions of kinds of light were all the color of the *atimuktaka* flower; various and innumerable, the rays were subtle and soft, as pure, fragrant, and clean as the interior of a lotus, pervading the ten directions with unimpeded penetration.

From within the lotus pedestal emerges a wondrous pavilion, sustained by the Buddha and equal in extent to the Dharma-realm. It has the appearance of liberation, which is the bliss of quiescent extinction; it is empty, signless, wishless, unconditioned, uncreated, unborn, and undying; it is equal to the three periods of time, entirely enters the realm of emptiness, and transcends the sphere of the eye.

Mañjuśrī sat upright with his body straight upon the pavilion; with an unshakable mind, he contemplated the realm of the Buddha, personally realized the dharma of emptiness, attained the Vajra-samādhi, skillfully studied the teachings of Śākyamuni Buddha, decisively accomplished the objectless samādhi (anālambana-samādhi), and deeply entered the wisdom of the Buddha.

Mañjuśrī, together with all the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas, having performed Buddha-works throughout the worlds of the ten directions, delighted their hearts in the True Dharma and constantly and diligently cultivated it. Furthermore, they had long planted roots of goodness within the teachings of the Buddhas of the past; all were sustained by Mañjuśrī’s empowerment, their resolve for Bodhi never faltering, remaining like lions upon their fearless thrones.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Go and tell the assembly of bhikṣus at Jetavana and the bhikṣuṇīs of Śrāvastī that the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, now wishes to preach the Dharma."
He caused the upāsakas and upāsikās of Śrāvastī, whose roots of goodness in faith and devotion to the Triple Gem had fully matured, to all assemble together at once to listen to the Dharma.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda went from his monastic cell and his walking path, announcing everywhere:
"The Buddha wishes to teach the Dharma.
Some bhikṣus who had already gathered heard him, while others remained in their cells and each said:
"Having already seen the light and signs of the Dharma being preached, why is it that we are unable to go there?
Ānanda asked again,
"For what reason do they not come?"
The bhikṣus said:
"We now see that the Jeta Grove is filled with great water; there are no trees to be seen, only radiance, so we do not yet dare to depart."
At that time, Ānanda went to where the Buddha was and said to him:
“World-Honored One,
the bhikṣus are unable to come.”

Why is this? Because they saw that the Great Grove of Jeta was entirely filled with pure, stainless water, and they could no longer see the monastery or its trees; for this reason, none of them were able to come.
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"Those bhikṣus perceive the notion of water where there is no water; they perceive the notion of form within what is not form; they perceive the notions of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness within what is not feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; and they perceive the notions of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas within what are not śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas."
"Ānanda! Go once more and summon all the bhikṣus; let them come from their monastic cells and walking paths to listen to the Dharma.
At that time, Ānanda, having received the Buddha’s instruction, went to the kingdom of Śrāvastī and commanded the bhikṣus, as well as the bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās:
“The World-Honored One now intends to preach the Dharma and has sent me to summon you; you should go quickly to listen.
Thereupon, the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās all assembled together before the Buddha.
The Buddha told Maudgalyāyana:

"You should now, together with the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas of the trichiliocosm, set forth in great adornment. The bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās—all of whom are intent upon the Mahāyāna—as well as the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans, have all assembled and come to hear the Dharma; those who have not heard it before shall now hear it in its entirety."

Gods, humans, and asuras all came to listen to the Dharma; they had already planted roots of goodness under immeasurable Buddhas of the past and set out upon the Mahāyāna. For those seeking the Mahāyāna, it is the most supreme vehicle, also called the foremost pure vehicle. Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, having donned the great armor to adorn themselves, practice this vehicle and universally proclaim it so that all may know and assemble at this gathering.
Maudgalyāyana replied to the Buddha, “So be it, World-Honored One!

Then, in the time it takes a strong man to bend and extend his arm, he traveled throughout the trichiliocosm. At all the sites of the great adornments of the bodhisattvas, and among the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās, as well as the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans, they all heard and understood through the Buddha’s supernatural power and the power of his vows.
He immediately returned to where the Buddha was and said to him:
"World-Honored One!
I have informed them all."

At that time, the fourfold assembly gathered like clouds, extending for a thousand yojanas in length and breadth and rising five thousand yojanas in height; they filled the land of Central India, their hearts joyfully longing to hear the Dharma.
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
the fourfold assembly has already gathered.”
At that time, the devas filled the void of space; all joined their palms and addressed the Buddha, saying:

“Now this great assembly is all struck with awe and fear; out of reverence for the Tathāgata’s majestic virtue, they dare not sit down at will. We only pray that the World-Honored One will grant them leave to sit.”

At that time, the Tathāgata manifested a portentous sign: in a single kṣaṇa, there emerged from the earth hundreds of thousands of millions of *jambūnada* golden lotuses with billions of petals, their radiance blazing like a treasury of fire, with stalks of celestial lapis lazuli, pericarps of red pearls, and stems of the seven treasures.
The entire great assembly each knew for themselves that they were seated before the Tathāgata.

The bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, non-humans, and others all faced the Buddha, gazing up at the World-Honored One.

At that time, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva was the foremost leader, and all the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas adorned their bodies with the thirty-two marks; their complexions were like pure gold, and they were courageous, diligent, and possessed of blazing majesty and virtue.

At that time, the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, including Mañjuśrī and the others, all rose from their lotus pedestals and, with palms joined toward the Buddha, entreated the World-Honored One to focus his mind single-mindedly on mindfulness of the Buddha.
At that time, Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

The fourfold assembly has all gathered and is settled in silence; all the devas fill the void of space. We only pray that the World-Honored One will extensively expound the Dharma-wheel of pure non-retrogression.”

At that time, there were bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās, and immeasurable hundreds of thousands of devas—those who practice through faith and those who practice through the Dharma, as well as the eight classes of noble ones—who conceived the notions of being srotāpannas, sakṛdāgāmins, anāgāmins, arhats, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and Buddhas, each forming this thought:
"May the Buddha expound the teaching to comfort our minds."

For what reason and by what causes do you speak of those who practice through faith, those who practice through the Dharma, up to the eight types of noble persons—the stream-enterer, the once-returner, the non-returner, and the arhat?
"For what reason do you speak thus?
The World-Honored One remained silent.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
During the latter part of the night, as dawn was about to break, I rose from my seat, left my dwelling, and went straight to the room of Mañjuśrī.”

Having arrived, he first entered the house and saw ten thousand lotus flowers emerge all around from within the Tathāgata’s chamber; celestial drums resounded spontaneously, and the sound of singing was heard. He beheld the Jeta Grove, the city of Śrāvastī, and the trichiliocosm, all universally illuminated by radiance.
"For what cause and condition has this auspicious omen appeared now?
After Śāriputra had spoken these words, the Buddha immediately told him:
"It is for the sake of preaching the Dharma that I have first manifested this auspicious sign."
At that time, Mañjuśrī questioned the Tathāgata:
"What Dharma do you intend to teach that this omen has first appeared?
Then Ānanda again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

During the latter part of the night, when the sky was about to brighten, light entered through my window. Having seen it, I immediately rose from my seat and went out of my room. I saw that the Jeta Grove was filled with pure water, stainless and unclouded; no trees, vihāras, or monastic cells were visible, but only a great radiance.”
"For what cause and for what reason has this auspicious omen appeared first?
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Ānanda, saying:
"The Tathāgata is about to expound the Wheel of the Pure Dharma; this is also a sign of auspiciousness resulting from the spiritual power and exhortation of Mañjuśrī."
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses for Mañjuśrī:
“This vehicle is pure, and through it one attains Buddha-wisdom;
Mañjuśrī, with his wondrous eloquence, has raised questions on this meaning.”
The One Vehicle is stainless; having attained the supreme wisdom of a Buddha, Mañjuśrī manifests it and thus poses this question.
The vehicle is non-discriminative and free from all conceptual proliferation.
Mañjuśrī, in order to manifest this, has therefore asked such a question:
"There is fundamentally no coming, nor is there any going;
it is just like nirvāṇa," as Mañjuśrī has asked.
In reality, there is no attainment of fruit, nor is there anything taught;
it is only through skillful means that sentient beings are guided.
One remains far removed from sounds, for sound itself is but a single characteristic.
Mañjuśrī, in order to manifest this, has therefore posed this question.
Seeking sound by means of sound, there is no sound to be grasped;
the names and words of sound are empty—this is what Mañjuśrī has asked.
This sound is like the wind, having no place of dependence;
sound itself is liberation—this is what Mañjuśrī has asked.
Ānanda, listen attentively!
The questions asked by Mañjuśrī;
skillful means and bodhi—these are all non-existent.
Both the Buddha and bodhi are mere sounds, devoid of reality.
Nor do they have any location; all phenomena are thus.
Awakening is formless, for causes and conditions are unarisen;
there is no coming or going—this is what the Buddhas have taught.
Unconditioned and signless, like space it is invisible;
enlightenment is ineffable—this is what Mañjuśrī has asked.
For all Buddhas of the past, future, and present, it is exactly thus.
Wisdom has no location; it is neither heard nor seen.
Its nature and characteristics are thus, manifesting the Dharma-realm;
yet by means of provisional names, it reveals the ultimate reality.
Cultivating pure giving, maintaining precepts without flaw;
firm in patience, they resolve to seek Bodhi.
Diligent without slackening, they practice dhyāna to collect the mind.
With pure wisdom, they seek bodhi.
The Buddha, through skillful means, delivers all by means of supernormal powers;
for those sentient beings who have no refuge, he preaches bodhi.
Distinguishing the three vehicles and the differences between the four fruits;
with the wisdom of suchness, he saves the world according to what is appropriate.
He manifests in lands of the five turbidities for the sake of those who are inferior.
Regarding the path of the One Vehicle, they were startled, doubtful, and did not believe it.
Therefore, the four fruits were taught to reveal the stage of the Arhat;
through the gate of the Śrāvaka, they enter the gate of the Buddha's teaching.
Explaining the calculable and the incalculable through the distinctions of causes and conditions;
directly perceiving the Four Noble Truths, they realize the characteristics of all dharmas.
These are the śrāvakas and arhats, as well as the pratyekabuddhas.
Attaining together the non-arising of phenomena, these are called Bodhisattvas.
Practicing the samādhis of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness;
they enter the gates of liberation and dwell securely in nirvāṇa.
Regarding the limits of the past, future, and present, the mind has no attachments;
it can open up the ten directions, which are unborn and unconditioned.
Such profound dharmas as these were [taught to] Ānanda and Mañjuśrī.
Employing skillful means to pose questions through the power of signless wisdom,
they ride the path of the Single Vehicle and realize that all phenomena are signless;
for this reason, they question the Buddha, who now explains the various fruits.
The three periods of time are equal, known as empty and signless;
all sounds are quiescent, for there is no Buddha-enlightenment.
There are worlds of Buddhas as numerous as the sands of countless Ganges Rivers.
They have come seeking Bodhi, summoned by Mañjuśrī.
Having heard of the practices of those Buddhas and Bodhisattvas,
and desiring to preach the Three Vehicles, they have gathered in the Sahā world.
Mañjuśrī poses the question to resolve doubts;
distinguishing the fruition of the vehicle, he requests an exposition on bodhi.
By the Buddha’s spiritual power and the force of his vow;
Therefore, the three vehicles are taught to deliver sentient beings from suffering.
May they diligently practice the eloquence of Mañjuśrī;
may the world-saving discourse explain the conduct of the bodhisattvas.
Billions of devas make offerings to the Savior of the World;
for those who conceive the thought of him as a fruit-bearing tree, he comforts their doubts.
Such bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs, as well as laymen and laywomen of pure faith—
He manifests the marks of supreme excellence.
Responding to Mañjuśrī’s inquiry, he comforts those in doubt;
these bodhisattvas have come for the sake of the Dharma.

2. Chapter on Faith and Practice. The Sūtra of the Non-Retrogression Dharma-Wheel, Chapter Two: Faith and Practice. At that time, after the World-Honored One had spoken these verses, Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Does the Tathāgata now turn the non-retrogressive dharma-wheel for Mañjuśrī?"
When he had asked this question, the Buddha said, "So it is, so it is!
Ānanda then addressed the Buddha again, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Is the Tathāgata now turning the wheel of the Dharma of non-retrogression?
The Buddha said:
"So it is, so it is, Ānanda! The Tathāgata truly turns the irreversible wheel of Dharma."
Ānanda again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"By what skillful means does the Tathāgata speak of these eight classes of practitioners—the faith-follower and the dharma-follower; the srotāpanna, sakṛdāgāmin, anāgāmin, arhat, śrāvaka, and pratyekabuddha—and for all such persons, does the Tathāgata reveal them as being the Dharma of the bodhisattva?"
For what reason, then, does it further say:

"For the sake of inferior beings born in the five turbid worlds who do not understand the Mahāyāna, the Tathāgata, having attained mastery in skillful means, perceives that among all sentient beings those with the great mind are few and most harbor inferior inclinations"?

Therefore, World-Honored One, you know their faculties and natures, and you reveal the Buddha-dharma through skillful means to deliver them; you teach and transform sentient beings with immeasurable wholesome dharmas, causing them to extinguish all sufferings and bring an end to birth and death, freeing them from all decline and affliction so that they may abide in the realization of unconditioned nirvana, and even enabling them to attain all-knowledge.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Ānanda, saying:

"A Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, for the sake of immeasurable and boundless sentient beings, causes them to give rise to faith and understanding regarding the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, as well as the dharmas known by countless Buddhas—from formlessness down to feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—which are undefiled and unattached; this is called 'faithful practice' (śraddhā-caryā)."
Furthermore, Ānanda!
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to believe that all dharmas are empty according to the Tathāgata and forms such an understanding, this is also called the bodhisattva’s practice of faith.

When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva places faith in the Buddha’s wisdom and gives rise to joy in their heart, they wonder, "What is this wisdom? Since they do not perceive any phenomena at all, and because of this non-perception, it is called the stage of practice through faith (*śraddhācaryā*).
Furthermore, Ānanda,
when a bodhisattva mahāsattva is not defiled by the five desires and does not abandon their faith, this is called the "faith-practice" (śraddhācaryā) of a bodhisattva.
Furthermore, the bodhisattva mahāsattva reflects as follows:
"To bestow the inconceivable Dharma upon all sentient beings, just like the mark of Suchness"—
one who can believe in such inconceivable giving of the Dharma is called a Bodhisattva of faith-practice (śraddhā-caryā).

Because of their joy, Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are able to relinquish their own bodies without weariness or satiety; they do not give rise to envy or anger toward anything; all that they practice as giving they dedicate, and having made such dedication, they do not even grasp at the notion of awakening, because it is indestructible. This is called the bodhisattva’s practice of faith.
"Furthermore, Ānanda!

When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, with pure faith and right mindfulness, is directed toward the Buddha, his mind is free from defilement and his faith is likewise stainless. All dharmas are equal; there is no sentient being, no life-span, no self, and no person; there are no aggregates, elements, or sense-bases. Furthermore, he himself does not cling to the locus of a life-span. This is called liberation through the practice of faith."

To transform and teach sentient beings so that they may have faith in the Buddha-dharma, and with a disciplined mind dedicate their merit toward Bodhi; furthermore, not perceiving the characteristics of the mind, being able to know that the six elements, the aggregates, and the sense bases are equal and identical to the Dharma-realm; because of this non-discrimination, one knows that the Dharma-realm has no differentiated marks—this is called the gift of faith.

"All things are impermanent; all conditioned phenomena are suffering; all conditioned phenomena are empty; all conditioned phenomena are without self. Within these teachings, one attains the power of wisdom, believes in giving, believes in the noble precepts and the precepts free from frivolous proliferation, attains the power of meditative concentration, and believes in the realm of cessation. This is called a bodhisattva who believes in giving.

Although they teach and transform sentient beings, they always maintain faith in quiescence; yet they do not grasp at the marks of sentient beings. They contemplate all sentient beings as identical to quiescence, skillfully knowing that all sentient beings are signless, entirely equal to the Dharma-realm, neither seen nor unseen.
Why is this? Because the dharma-realm is precisely the mind-realm of all sentient beings; this is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s practice of faith.
"Furthermore, Ānanda!..."

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva contemplates that all sentient beings lack any reality; they have no abiding and no cessation, for their nature and characteristics are fundamentally empty. Therefore, he does not perceive any sentient beings and finds no place of reliance, contemplating all sentient beings as identical to the realm of Nirvāṇa.
Why is this? Because all sentient beings enter the realm of emptiness.
That a bodhisattva can cause such immeasurable sentient beings to all give rise to faith and understanding is called the "faith-practice" of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke these verses:
“Sentient beings with great faith see countless Buddhas;
Not clinging to the marks of form—this is called the practice of faith.”
To have faith in all dharmas, to reveal the characteristic of emptiness,
and to achieve liberation— this is called the practice of faith.
Always believing in the True Dharma and joyfully seeking the Buddha;
When shall I attain inconceivable wisdom? Observing the five desires, I find nothing in them worthy of trust;
having attained the power of faith, this is called the practice of faith.
Such faith is most excellent; one should practice the gift of Dharma and make offerings to the Great Sage.
Through this inconceivable giving, one attains the eloquence of faith.
To be free from thoughts of inferiority is called the practice of faith.
To completely relinquish the body one holds dear,
yet to have no thought of relinquishment, is called the practice of faith.
Able to give all things, harboring no envy;
having relinquished the notion of enlightenment—this is called the practice of faith.
With a pure mind of faith, free from all turbidity and defilement;
Nor is there any life-span; this is called the practice of faith.
Although one practices giving, one does not seek its karmic reward;
attaining the power of deep faith, this is called the practice of faith.
Abandoning the six sense bases and not dwelling on their karmic retribution;
skillfully understanding the six elements—this is called the practice of faith.
Having disciplined oneself, one also disciplines others.
To cause one to have faith in the Buddha-dharma is called the practice of faith.
Having attained this faith, to dedicate it toward Bodhi,
yet without any mental characteristics, is called the practice of faith.
Knowing that the six elements are entirely identical to the dharma-realm;
though one speaks of the dharma-realm, its characteristics as an element cannot be apprehended.
All conditioned phenomena are impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self.
Nor does one grasp at them; this is called the practice of faith.
Being able to believe in the noble precepts and being free from all frivolous proliferation;
achieving meditative concentration—this is called the practice of faith.
To believe that all sentient beings share the same mark of quiescence,
and having realized this marklessness, is called the practice of faith.
Not clinging to sentient beings, they enter together into the Dharma-realm.
This realm of sentient beings is inconceivable.
To give rise to faith through faith is called "faith";
for a bodhisattva to be fearless is called "the practice of faith."
Sentient beings are determined to have no perception of existence;
their essential nature is like space, with no location and no realization.
Both sentient beings and nirvana are empty.
To give rise to faith therein is called the practice of faith.
The fearless Bodhisattva has faith in all sentient beings;
they do not grasp at names and forms, for these arise from faith.
One who can believe thus, constantly mindful and never losing it;
Ānanda, you should remember and uphold it, revealing and analyzing it.
Such dharmas are immeasurable and innumerable.
That which the Buddha has realized and awakened to,
the Bodhisattva manifests. "Furthermore, Ānanda,
when the Tathāgata, the Arhat, fully explains such profound meanings through the power of faith, this is called the 'course of faith' (śraddhācaryā) of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva."
At that time, the World-Honored One, seeing that the faith and resolve of all sentient beings were firm and steadfast, spoke again in verse:
"All who hear this, Their hearts shall be filled with joy;
Such are the merits spoken of By these sons of the Buddhas."
The manifestation of the Bodhisattva is inconceivable;
it inspires faith in those who do not believe in the Bodhi of all Buddhas.
It is unstained by provisional names and devoid of mental factors.
Not clinging to the ten directions is called supreme faith.
The Bodhisattva proclaims it clearly, constantly cultivating the dharma of faith;
not grasping at emptiness, they manifest quiescent extinction.
As taught by the Savior of the World, liberation is thus;
the characteristics of form are likewise, as taught, so should one practice.
The Bodhisattva has clearly explained this, and the wise are able to believe it.
The Buddha is inconceivable, with immeasurable mindfulness.
What the Bodhisattvas believe in is as boundless as space;
the Buddha’s wisdom is measureless, and he is titled the Great Man.
Aiming for non-attachment, they do not commit unwholesome acts out of greed, yet they relinquish attachment to worldly dharmas.
This is called a bodhisattva who is able to practice the gift of Dharma;
the faith of such a bodhisattva is sealed by the excellent vow.
The gift of Dharma is inconceivable; one gives food and drink out of faith, as well as mani-jewels, gold, elephants, horses, carriages, servants, and the like.
One renounces wives, sons, daughters, and all kingdoms that belong to oneself.
The limbs, hands, feet, and joints, the head, eyes, marrow, and brain, the eyes,
ears, nose, and tongue— these are the supreme objects of faith for a bodhisattva;
they relinquish their bodies without attachment, yet do not even think of practicing giving.
In the past, I practiced the gift of Dharma in order to seek the wisdom of the Buddha;
I gave away my body without attachment, joyfully offering everything.
Constantly accompanied by spiritual friends, I cast off this fragile and precarious body.
Among all sentient beings, their faith is ever pure;
hearing the Dharma, they believe in all Buddhas—such a one is called a bodhisattva.
They know that the eyes, ears, nose, tongue, and the faculty of the body are all impermanent.
Impermanent as a mass of foam, they have deep faith and cast off their bodies;
for the sake of sentient beings who have no refuge, they establish the four means of integration.
With a heart of loving-kindness toward all, they place their trust in the Buddha’s immeasurable wisdom.
Seeing sentient beings who commit evil, he gives rise to the unsurpassed mind.
With deep faith in bodhi, he does not grasp at the characteristics of the mind;
yet sentient beings do not seek the Way, remaining deluded by the six elements.
That is to say, regarding all that is real, though there are no realms, they speak of the characteristics of realms;
seeing sentient beings in the cycle of transmigration, the deluded are attached to various extremes.
The Bodhisattva believes in non-self and that all conditioned phenomena are impermanent.
Seeing those who break the precepts, they take faith and the precepts as inconceivable;
establishing pure precepts and meditative concentration, the Bodhisattva dwells in the gathering of the mind.
If they see those who are indolent, they seek the Buddha’s power of diligence.
Mastery over all samādhis, The dhāraṇī of the wisdom of the True Dharma;
Fools are attached to the life-span, But one contemplates the aggregates as having no self that lives.
The nature of sentient beings is quiescent, And the characteristics of all phenomena are likewise so.
Believe that the aggregates have no coming or going, yet the karma of good and evil is never severed.
Due to pure and impure karma, one does not escape birth and death;
sentient beings share the same dharma-realm, and the dharma-realm is itself birth and death.
This is called the inconceivable, the fearless faith of the bodhisattva;
it is the supreme, inconceivable faith that consists in diligent cultivation of the Dharma-knowledge.
It is not for those of meager wisdom that this is called the teaching of pure faith.
All sentient beings who share this same faith Dwell eternally in non-existence.
In emptiness they have no attachment; They do not abide in any phenomena.
Sentient beings are empty, and that emptiness is also empty— They are identical with the realm of nirvāṇa.
He preaches the Dharma as always being signless, causing sentient beings to have faith and understanding;
seeing that the nature of all phenomena is empty, he regards all sentient beings with equanimity.
Possessing supreme wisdom within the three realms of existence, he attains such faith and upholds it.
This is also called supreme faith, delighting in the Dharma that is free from fear.
Among those wise ones within the Buddha-dharma, they have confidence in themselves and encourage others to have confidence;
thus teaching one another in succession, they increase all merits.
With a pure mind free from attachment, one serves as a field of merit for the benefit of others;
rejoicing in self-discipline and generosity, in pure precepts and patience,
in diligence, meditative concentration, and so forth, with wisdom as the guiding light.
Through skillful means he manifests pure wisdom, causing sentient beings to attain supreme bliss.
At the end of his life, he leaves behind the evil realms; the Bodhisattva’s wisdom is most excellent.
Through supernormal powers he transforms sentient beings, and the world shakes in six ways.
The light shines universally everywhere, the wondrous wisdom of the Bodhisattvas;
With the signless lion’s roar, throughout the east, west, south, and north,
And in the four intermediate directions as well as above and below, The sound of the Dharma issues forth from all.
Vowing to have no doubt regarding the Buddha, they likewise cause others to do so.
By reason of these causes and conditions, immeasurable marks are manifested;
that the wise one abides herein can only be realized and known by a Buddha.
