Recorded in the *Sengyou lu* as a distinct scripture from the Liang region by Master Dao’an.
In the second translation from the *Beiliang lu*, following the "Chapter on Faithful Practice" (*śraddhācaryā*): "Ānanda!
This is called the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha’s skillful means for expounding faithful practice to all bodhisattvas."
Ānanda asked, “In what way does the Tathāgata further teach the practice of the Dharma to the bodhisattvas?
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"You should now know this!

A bodhisattva mahāsattva does not dwell in the Buddha-dharmas, yet is able to manifest them as never departing from the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu), reaching the ultimate inconceivable realm, and upholding all dharmas with a mind free from inferiority;
though they expound all dharmas, they have no grasping or attachment to the characteristics of dharmas, being without thought and without dwelling."
He upholds the dharmas as they truly are in their essential nature; he neither grasps at dharmas nor rejects non-dharmas; he does not delight in dharmas, nor does he not delight in dharmas.

Although he is thus able to remain detached from the characteristics of all dharmas, his mind is well-tamed and ever-abiding in peace and joy. He skillfully expounds all dharmas without agitation, and regarding the characteristics of all dharmas, he is neither separate from the body nor dwelling within the body. This body’s prior limit is equal to the dharma-realm; like space, it has no coming or going, and it is identical to the reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*) and the mark of suchness (*tathatā*). This is what the Buddha taught for Bodhisattvas to realize and know: pure and stainless, contemplating all dharmas as empty, without seeing, and without grasping.
Why is this? Because they are non-existent, detached, and unattached.

One does not perceive any phenomena; there is nothing to grasp and no contention. The Dharma-realm is manifested as beyond words and speech; its essential nature is fundamentally empty, and the sphere of mental activity has ceased. This mind cannot be apprehended and is inconceivable; it merely demonstrates the realm of quiescent extinction and non-conditionality, upholding all phenomena without any basis of dependence.
Why is this? Because all dharmas are without substance and without marks.

This dharma of the bodhisattva is of a single mark, which is marklessness; it is beyond praise and is a teaching of non-fruition. If, for the sake of others, one speaks of the marks, names, and all phrases of the dharma, having already personally realized them, and achieves this dharma, one is called a bodhisattva mahāsattva of the lineage.

Having attained this lineage, one regards all phenomena as neither coming nor going, neither grasping nor abandoning; one upholds all phenomena without movement or decay. Because they are indestructible, this is called the practice of the Dharma (dharmacaryā).
"Because of the accomplishment of the Dharma, one sees that all phenomena are signless; because of attaining the benefit of the Dharma, it is also called 'Dharma-practice'.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"The Dharma is without regression, and so too are all Buddhas."
If one can uphold this, it is called practicing the Dharma.
To manifest the Buddha-dharma as formless and signless,
profoundly deep and unstained— this is called practicing the Dharma.
Not departing from the various realms is itself the inconceivable;
reaching the Dharma-realm is called the practice of the Dharma.
To protect and uphold all dharmas as the Buddha has revealed—this is the practice of the Dharma.
A mind free from blemish and defilement is called the practice of the Dharma.
Turning the wheel of non-retrogression is called signlessness;
not grasping or clinging to it is called the practice of the Dharma.
Without grasping and without dwelling, one upholds the wisdom of the Dharma;
one who maintains it in this way is said to practice the Dharma.
With a mind always full of delight, one seeks the Dharma without weariness.
To remain far removed from indolence is called practicing the Dharma.
Hearing the Dharma and upholding it, being untainted and without dependence;
dwelling well in peace and bliss—this is called practicing the Dharma.
If one who preaches the Dharma does not think of it nor cling to it,
but upholds it as signless, this is called "practice of the Dharma.
With a virtuous body and virtuous abiding, one dwells in no fixed location.
This body is no-body; this is called knowing the characteristic of the body.
Being without prior or posterior limits, it is equal to the dharma-nature;
being without going or coming, this is called knowing the characteristic of the body.
Just as the Buddhas manifest the bodhisattvas,
having attained this Dharma, it is called "Dharma-practice.
The nature and characteristics of the realm of space are entirely without attachment.
To be able to uphold [the Dharma] in this way is called "practice according to the Dharma.
Furthermore, regarding all phenomena, one perceives emptiness and sees nothing;
if there is nothing seen, then there is no obstruction.
Manifesting the signless, there is no contention;
without words and without speech, there is likewise nothing that exists.
Free from all mental characteristics, there is nothing to be attained.
If the mind has no attainment, it is called inconceivable.
Without coming and without going, yet not being unmanifest;
without conditions and without explanation, it is called inconceivable.
If one upholds this Dharma, it cannot be relied upon;
it is called "non-existence," and this is what is meant by "upholding the Dharma.
Such is the Dharma as taught by the Bodhisattvas.
Without conjunction and without dispersion, it reveals non-action;
this is called the sphere of practice, the sphere of the spiritual lineage.
Attaining such benefit is called the sphere of practice.
From this lineage, there is nothing to be censured;
attaining such a realm is called "upholding the Dharma.
Seeing that the Dharma does not diminish, though one acts, there is no going away.
Coming yet not coming, no dharma is perceived;
whether coming or going, all dharmas are likewise.
Holding the Dharma in this way, there is no wavering.
Neither increasing nor decreasing, this is the unconditioned dharma;
if there is neither increase nor decrease, this is called upholding the dharma.
The characteristics of dharmas are suchness—without conditions and without explanation.
One who attains this Dharma is called a "Upholder of the Dharma.
Therefore, Ānanda, manifest the Bodhisattva!
To attain the benefit of the profound Dharma is called "upholding the Dharma.
Therefore, Ānanda, manifest this upholding of the Dharma!
For those who lack faith, he preaches this Dharma;
making such distinctions, he speaks for the sake of bodhisattvas;
all through skillful means, he reveals and elucidates the Buddha-dharma.
"Thus it is, Ānanda! The Tathāgata, the Perfectly Awakened One, has taught this skillful means for the sake of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas to reveal the upholding of the Dharma.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"How does the Tathāgata teach the Dharma of the Eightfold Noble Path for the sake of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas?
How do the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas distance themselves from the eight wrong paths, turn toward the eight liberations, and transcend the state of ordinary beings?"
They cultivate the Eightfold Noble Path, yet without reaching any destination; they remain far removed from all extremes, dwelling in the Middle Way.
They transcend the stage of ordinary beings and abide securely in Bodhi, yet they do not dwell even on the mark of Bodhi.
Free from all false views, they cultivate right view; they do not grasp at the marks of the body, nor do they dwell on the marks of Bodhi.

The Buddha-body is unconditioned and transcends all numerical categories. One who cultivates the marks of a Buddha attains the single mark of sentient beings—which is marklessness—and emerges from the aggregates, elements, and sense bases of birth-and-death.
Abiding securely in the house of ultimate emptiness, which is unconditioned, they perceive that all phenomena are without arising and without abiding.
Why is this? Because the nature and characteristics of all phenomena are entirely without abiding.
They are far removed from both the mundane and the supramundane, dwelling in the state of quiescent extinction.
They are unstained by the mundane world and unattached to the supramundane;
they remain far removed from both what is Dharma and what is non-Dharma, as well as from the conditioned and the unconditioned.

Having abandoned the extremes of annihilationism and eternalism, they abide in the mark of equality. They know that the mental factors of the past, future, and present possess no distinct characteristics, nor do they apprehend any characteristic of the bodhicitta.
Why is this? Because all states of mind are equal.
The same is true of the physical form; therefore, one cannot be harmed by poison, fire, swords, or arrows.
Why is this? Because they have already departed from all the poisons of affliction (*kleśa*).

They are constantly born in pure lands and remain free from all evil destinies (*durgati*); though they dwell within the various realms of existence, they realize *bodhi*. They abide eternally in peace and security, yet without any dependence. For these reasons, no weapons or arms can cause them harm.
Why is this? Because one perceives that the nirvana of bodhi is empty and has no place of abiding.
Because there is no abiding, all poisonous arrows cannot cause harm; this is called being unbound.
One who rides upon the swift vehicle yet does not abide in that vehicle is called "unbound. Why is this?
Because there is nothing to be attained; therefore, swords and arrows cannot harm their body.
Knowing that all phenomena are empty and cannot be apprehended, one cannot be harmed by any poison or injury. Why is this?
Because the practice of universal compassion pervades and covers all things.

One practices the compassion of awakening because no sentient beings can be apprehended; one practices the compassion of emptiness because all phenomena are quiescent; one practices the compassion free from fever because it is far removed from all afflictions.

Practicing such loving-kindness enables one to remain unharmed by weapons; it renders the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm entirely equal. One knows that the nature of all realms and all phenomena is identical to bodhi, being without any marks of difference. If one can thus maintain a mind free from discursive thought, without frivolity, it is tranquil, extinguished, and pure.

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva knows that all dharmas are like the sound of an echo; they are free from all marks, entirely identical with the Dharma-realm, without refuge and without destination. He skillfully understands all sounds and languages, yet there is nothing shown and nothing spoken, being free from the characteristics of sound. He does not exalt himself and is free from the notion of self. He transcends all speech and sounds, yet remains without the characteristic of transcendence. For this reason, he fully knows that all dharmas are quiescent and extinguished.

"Furthermore, one does not apprehend the characteristics of any phenomena; transcending all dharmas, the mind has no place of return, and one is likewise unstained by or attached to any sounds or speech.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"Avoiding the eight wrong paths, One cultivates the eightfold right path;"
The nine stages and eight liberations are called the Eight Ranks.
Transcending the state of ordinary beings yet not dwelling in [the limited] bodhi—
these heroes among dharmas are called the Eight Ranks.
Transcending ordinary beings yet not dwelling in bodhi;
detached from the marks of bodhi—this is called the eight classes of noble ones.
Abandoning all false views, they practice right view.
Having already reached the Way, they are called the Eightfold Assembly.
Having transcended all bodily marks, they do not dwell in bodhi;
having detached from the realization of the Buddha-body, they are called the Eightfold Assembly.
Free from the notion of sentient beings, they constantly cultivate the notion of the Buddha;
transcending the notion of meditative concentration—these are called the eight ranks.
Free from the lair of sentient beings, they enter the city of Nirvana.
All dharmas are without abiding; these are called the eight classes.
Having emerged from the world, they reveal the noble path;
having realized the realm of quiescent extinction, these are called the eight classes.
Detached from all worldly things, they proclaim the characteristics of the Buddha-dharma;
with no realization in their minds, these are called the Eightfold Assembly.
There is no limit of existence, nor is there a limit of non-existence.
To remain far removed from existence and non-existence is called the Eightfold Path.
To be tranquil and unconditioned, to abandon the extremes of annihilationism and eternalism,
and to enter deeply into equanimity— this is called the Eightfold Path.
They do not grasp at past or future minds;
the same applies to the present. These are called the eight ranks.
It is said that there is an initial mind from which bodhicitta is generated.
The characteristics of the mind are inherently empty; how can it be called bodhi?
There is no arrival and no departure, nor is there any bodhi;
it cannot be harmed by poison, fire, swords, or arrows.
Severing all realms of existence, forever free from dependence;
neither coming nor going, yet without causing harm.
Without orientation toward enlightenment, they proclaim the sound of the teaching.
Realizing suchness for oneself, not through the instruction of another;
neither attaining this destination nor any non-destination;
sounds perishing moment by moment—the Mahāyāna is swiftly revealed.
He constantly teaches the peaceful and secure, the supreme Dharma of emptiness;
if one can swiftly realize it, this is called being "unfettered.
By swiftly mounting this Dharma, one receives the prediction of a bodhisattva.
With a mind free from abandonment, this is called being unbound.
One will not be invaded or oppressed by weapons or the evil realms;
having attained fearlessness in body, poison cannot harm them.
The Bodhisattva practices loving-kindness, pervading all;
being free from contention and dispute, this is called "unfettered.
Not grasping at the marks of the body, they skillfully discern the body.
Having reached the path to enlightenment, they abandon the evil realms;
having eliminated their ignorance, they possess mastery of supernormal powers;
having attained the light of bodhi—these are called the eight classes of noble ones.
Knowing the realms of desire and form, as well as the formless;
that the three realms share the same characteristic—this is called the eightfold assembly.
All realms are equal; this is the awakening free from affliction.
Delusive thoughts and ignorance cannot defile them;
they transcend all signs and are beyond reproach.
Whatever they may speak, it all tends toward the Dharma-realm.
To speak of having no destination is to be identical with the Dharma-realm;
when the mind abides in the patience of the Dharma, this is called the Eightfold Assembly.
If one wishes to practice, one should abide in the dharma of quiescent extinction.
Not praising oneself while speaking for others;
transcending the characteristics of sound and crossing over the characteristics of sound;
not clinging to sounds—this is called the eightfold assembly.
Through liberation by means of sound, one knows that dharmas are signless;
they have no place of abiding, no coming, and no going.
Ānanda, you should know that such are these eight classes of beings.
"Among all teachings, this is the foremost.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Ānanda, saying:
"You should now know!"
"The Tathāgata, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, has skillfully taught and demonstrated these eight classes for the sake of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
Ānanda asked: "In what way, World-Honored One, does the Tathāgata teach the srotāpanna for the sake of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas?"
The Buddha said:
“One who is a *srotāpanna* (stream-enterer) has attained entry into the flow of the noble path; this is called the inconceivable Buddha-dharma.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva can practice in this way—without perceiving the path or that which is practiced on the path—they transcend all marks (*nimitta*). They flow into the Buddha-dharma, which is neither form nor birth. They have no attachment to any dharma; all dharmas have no location, no conditions, no abiding, no existence, and are not established.”

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva reaches this path, they attain firm diligence, firm power, firm knowledge, and firm wisdom; they do not give rise to indolence, abide in tranquility, and ride upon the path of reality to provide supreme and unsurpassed protection for sentient beings. They do not grasp at this path, nor do they dwell within it.

Cultivating such a path to seek all dharmas, they find nothing to be attained; they neither sink nor waver, and they are without the notion of dwelling, the notion of a path, the notion of the world, or the notion of a Buddha.
All things are entirely equal and free from hindrances; their sphere of wise activity is without obstruction.

Abiding in the mark of equanimity toward all dharmas and all false views, opening the Buddha’s knowledge and vision to reveal the profound Dharma-gate, and discerning the view of a self-body to transcend the notion of "I"—this is called a Srotāpanna.

They do not grasp at the ultimate unimpededness of the Buddha-way, yet they joyfully seek the Buddha-way without being attached to precepts; nor do they grasp at the Buddha’s precepts, for they do not take up precepts through the grasping of rules, nor do they take up precepts by grasping at signs.

Having already abandoned the three fetters, they do not dwell within the triple world; practicing the noble path as the Buddha has taught, they are free from all conceptualizations and do not grasp at objects.
Being without any obstacles, they enter the Buddha-way, their minds attaining tranquility, and they do not cling to views such as those of a life-span, a self, or a person.

With the sense faculties purified and far removed from afflictions, they practice giving for the sake of cultivating bodhi; relinquishing everything to rescue suffering sentient beings, they cause them to cross the four torrents and establish them in nirvāṇa;
exhausting all marks of existence, they manifest the signless.

If one sees the fourfold assembly and does not give rise to fear, but resolutely seeks the path of quiescent, pure bodhi, having already abandoned all fears, there will be no fear of death. Why is this?

Directly realizing cessation and being free from all defilements, dwelling well in the Buddha-way while knowing that the destinies of the past and future are themselves without coming or going, yet skillfully discerning the perceptions of sentient beings, with a mind free from conceptual proliferation, one brings the Buddha-way to ultimate completion; this is called the mark of a *srotāpanna* bodhisattva-mahāsattva.
Chapter Three: On Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
“The Buddha’s teaching of the four paths is inconceivable;
if there are those who abide therein, they shall not regress from Bodhi.”
Just like space, it has no basis for support;
without abiding and without conditions, it is free from grasping and attachment.
This is called the Way, by which one attains a firm and steadfast mind.
Riding upon such a vehicle, the unsurpassed savior of the world does not abide in this or that, nor does he dwell in the middle stream;
being unattached even to the Buddha-way, he is called a Srotāpanna.
All the worlds, as well as all other dharmas of the Buddha;
having reached the ultimate further shore—this is named Srotāpanna.
Having extinguished all veils and hindrances, they manifest the path of the Buddha.
Exhausting all marks is called *srotāpanna*.
Without exalting oneself, one gives rise to the Buddha-dharma;
revealing and clarifying knowledge and vision, one enters the wisdom of the Buddha.
First they give rise to the notion of a self, which is a perversion and a multitude of evils;
having understood this, they do not cling to the Buddha-way.
Originally they doubted the Buddha, wondering whether he could be attained or not.
Ultimately free from attachment, they do not grasp at the notion of a path.
They do not give rise to the grasping for precepts, yet dwell well in the Buddha’s precepts;
they constantly cultivate right effort, yet do not grasp at the notion of precepts.
Having severed the three fetters, they are unattached to the triple world;
they practice the Buddha-way and understand the perceptions of sentient beings.
Though they cultivate bodhi, they do not grasp at such perceptions.
With mental activities stilled, one purifies the Buddha-way;
rejoicing in giving, one remains far removed from frowning;
abiding in right livelihood, the mind is free from frivolous proliferation.
Relinquishing everything to rescue suffering sentient beings,
attaining the unsurpassed gift, one is named a Srotāpanna;
having severed repeated birth, being signless and unattached.
Far removed from fear, they transcend worldly terrors;
having relinquished all that is both dharma and non-dharma,
and remaining unattached to the aggregates, they are called the light of the world.
Dwelling securely among the fourfold assembly, they are free from fear;
they manifest quiescent extinction and purely cultivate the Buddha-dharma.
They have no conception of a sentient being, nor do they hold the conception of reality.
This is called being unstained, yet discerning fear;
free from all fears, there is likewise no fear of death;
abiding in quiescence, one is stainless and secure.
Having already transcended the evil realms, they have no fear;
they skillfully expound all paths—those that are untainted and signless.
The Dharma of the Bodhisattva manifests as the stage of Srotāpanna.
For the sake of those who are inferior, I have made this statement;
through skillful means, I manifest the Buddha-dharma;
for the sake of those who are heedless, I reveal this teaching.
The World-Honored Savior teaches with many skillful means;
according to their original practices, he reveals the Buddha-way.
Ānanda, you should know that these are *srotāpannas*.
For those of small wisdom, I speak of such matters;
they do not understand skillful means, being foolish, narrow-minded, and inferior;
failing to recognize the profound, they give rise to contentious disputes.
"By means of hundreds of thousands of dharmas, he reveals the stage of srotāpanna;
as for the srotāpanna, it manifests the dharma of bodhi. Thus it is, Ānanda!"
"The Tathāgata, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, for the sake of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, has taught the stage of srotāpanna through skillful means.
Ānanda asked: "In what way does the Tathāgata, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, teach the stage of sakṛdāgāmin for the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas?"
“Ānanda, you should know!
A bodhisattva mahāsattva accords with wisdom; the Buddha-wisdom is inconceivable. They cultivate immeasurable causes, yet they do not grasp at the marks of those causes nor at the wisdom of bodhi.
They are able to sever all delusions while seeking the Buddha-wisdom, and they praise the vajra-samādhi as surpassing all other meditative concentrations.”
Extinguishing all fetters, afflictions, darkness, and obstructions, they see the Buddha everywhere and attain the impartial, correct contemplation of all Buddha-dharmas.

Seeking through immeasurable causes yet finding nothing to be attained, they act as the Buddhas do when realizing the Dharma: they do not stir sentient beings, nor do they stir the realm of sentient beings while grasping the dharma-realm.

For immeasurable sentient beings who have lacked much throughout vast eons and were unable to accomplish the path to Bodhi, he leads them to the stage of non-retrogression, causing them to aspire to the Buddha’s faculties, powers, factors of enlightenment, path, meditative concentrations, liberations, and formless absorptions.

I shall now, by means of such dharmas as these, reveal them to sentient beings so that they may attain understanding and seek the Buddha-way; desiring to sit at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) to seek the wisdom of reality (yathābhūta-jñāna), to penetrate the Buddha-eye and the inconceivable eye, and desiring to benefit all sentient beings by seeking the Buddha-eye—such wisdom is the most supreme.

He fully knows the profound characteristics of all phenomena, yet within his own wisdom he makes no discriminations; he establishes sentient beings so that they dwell within all phenomena, causing them to know that all phenomena are non-abiding. Because he has come to this assembly for the sake of attaining this Dharma, he is called a Sakṛdāgāmin.

Having arrived, one perceives the realm of sentient beings and the inconceivable realm with unimpeded penetration; since one does not grasp at objects, nor is there any attainment or reaching, how could there be the "accomplishing of sentient beings"?

Because one does not perceive the accomplishment of sentient beings, regarding all phenomena and the realm of sentient beings, one neither perceives nor does not perceive them; yet one knows that sentient beings flow into the dharma-realm and clearly understand the dharma-realm to be identical with bodhi.

One understands that the dharma-realm and the realm of sentient beings, as well as the immeasurable paths of the Buddhas, are without attainment and without discrimination, being identical to the wisdom of the path. Approaching peerless wisdom, free from defilement and pure, one attains that which is unattainable and realizes that which is unrealizable—this is called true wisdom.
"A Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva who seeks such wisdom is called a Sakṛdāgāmin.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"One who accords with this wisdom Is called 'inconceivable';"
For the sake of seeking the Buddha’s wisdom, he is therefore called a Sakṛdāgāmin.
Through immeasurable causes and conditions, he explains how to accomplish the path to Bodhi;
because he practices this Dharma, I constantly come and go to seek it.
The characteristics of the immovable samādhi eliminate the fetters of affliction;
therefore, by practicing it with single-minded devotion, one achieves accomplishment without regression.
One also knows what is Dharma and what is non-Dharma, penetrating the characteristic of unimpededness.
Abiding in the reality-limit of all phenomena, I cultivate the stage of the Sakṛdāgāmin.
In accordance with what the Buddha has taught, I practice exactly as I have heard;
For the sake of attaining this Dharma, I constantly come and go in search of it.
The Dharma-realm has never existed, yet it does not stir among sentient beings;
this is called a Sakṛdāgāmin, who has extinguished the marks of coming and going.
Sentient beings lack wisdom and suffer greatly from ignorance and delusion.
In order to establish [beings in the truth], they seek the wisdom of a Buddha;
Through the faculties, powers, factors of awakening, and so forth, as well as meditative concentrations and liberations;
Diligently cultivating the characteristics of samādhi, they seek the wisdom of a Buddha.
The ultimate path to enlightenment is that which all Buddhas have practiced;
this is called the stage of Sakṛdāgāmin, who practices and constantly seeks it.
If one attains such a Dharma, the Buddha-eye is inconceivable.
This is called a Sakṛdāgāmin, who constantly seeks the Buddha-eye.
Just as that which the Buddha sought, for the sake of providing refuge and reliance;
that which I now seek is the supreme omniscience.
That which is known by this wisdom is the true nature of all phenomena;
being unstained by and unattached to this wisdom, it is the supreme wisdom.
That which is known by this wisdom is the true nature of all phenomena.
With a mind forever free from defilement, one constantly seeks such a Dharma;
for the benefit and peace of all sentient beings, one abides in the supreme state of omniscience.
This is called a Sakṛdāgāmin, who seeks that which is attained through coming and going.
Contemplating the dharma-realm, one sees that sentient beings are inconceivable;
this is called a sakṛdāgāmin, who seeks the realm of sentient beings.
Having known the realm of sentient beings, they do not cling to sentient beings.
This is called a Sakṛdāgāmin, yet they seek that which is unobtainable.
If one does not perceive sentient beings, then all phenomena are signless;
being able to know thus, they guide and lead all sentient beings.
Though they contemplate all phenomena, they do not perceive the marks of observation;
with minds held steady and no distracted thoughts, they seek the teachings of all Buddhas.
Such pure wisdom is far removed from all defilements.
Not grasping at the characteristics of this wisdom—this is called seeking the Way.
To reveal and teach it to all sentient beings is what Bodhisattvas do not criticize;
this is called ultimate wisdom, and they have come for the sake of attaining it.

Ānanda, you should know: for those of little wisdom who are attached to the false appearances of right and wrong, I speak of the Sakṛdāgāmin. Ānanda, you should know: for those of little wisdom who are attached to the false appearances of right and wrong, I speak of the Sakṛdāgāmin.
May sentient beings who are diligent and energetic come to understand in this way:
by constantly and skillfully cultivating extensive learning and gaining certainty in the profound Dharma,
they shall attain the true meaning and swiftly achieve awakening.
“Ānanda! This is called the Tathāgata, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, skillfully teaching the fruit of once-returning (sakṛdāgāmin) for the sake of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. Ānanda said:
“What is meant by the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, teaching the state of an Anāgāmin for the sake of the Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas?
The Buddha told Ānanda:

“The Bodhisattva-mahāsattva transcends all worldly characteristics; having perfected the practice of a Buddha, his mind has no place of movement. Although he knows going and coming, he never grasps at the characteristics of going and coming. He knows that all dharmas have no basis upon which to dwell, and thus they neither come nor return.”
Why is this? Because one does not perceive that any phenomena have going or no-going.
One transcends ordinary beings and eliminates the notion of being an ordinary being; one does not cling to the notion of a Buddha and attains the dharma of non-abiding.
Why is this? Because they have reached the ultimate, quiescent Dharma-realm, wherein they do not perceive any distinguishing marks between Buddhas and ordinary beings.

They remain far removed from the evil realms and eliminate their craving; they do not cling to various flavors and are detached from the four kinds of nutriment. They reveal knowledge and vision, yet do not grasp at any of the sixty-two views. They do not see the existence of marks, nor do they cling to the markless; they are entirely free from both existence and non-existence.
Regarding all hindrances and obstacles, they manifest the aspect of *nirvāṇa*; being neither subject to transmigration nor exempt from it, they eliminate the defilements of the evil realms;

they subdue all Māras and distance themselves from ignorance; they extract the arrows of nescience and exhaust the seeds of nescience; they destroy the enemy of nescience and illuminate away greed and hatred; they sever all fetters and afflictions (*saṃyojana*) and reveal the true nature of all existences (*bhava*); they extract the arrows of craving and eliminate all pride; they thoroughly understand the characteristics of the aggregates (*skandha*) and reach the ultimate state of clarity; they constantly delight in the Buddha-vehicle and the inconceivable vehicle, arriving at the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva can thus emerge from the mire, become free from attachment, and attain the treasury of their original vows, they will also attain the treasuries of all past and future Buddhas. This is the supreme among all hidden treasures and was established by the Buddhas of the past. With a mind that is equanimous—neither high nor low—they attain such a vehicle which, for all sentient beings, is the most excellent, the foremost, the unsurpassed, and the ultimate Buddha-vehicle of the bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Having attained signlessness regarding all phenomena, the bodhisattva mahāsattva cuts through the web of doubt within all dharmas and realizes the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmin*).
Furthermore, Ānanda!

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, by means of the four great vows, gathers in all sentient beings and establishes all sentient beings, causing them all to enter the Buddha-vehicle and abide in the path to Bodhi.
How does one abide in bodhi?
It is said that by awakening to the characteristics of sentient beings as they truly are, one abides within the realm of sentient beings. Why is this?
One skillfully knows the realm of emptiness and the inconceivable realm as being free from the notion of a sentient being. Why is this?
Because the realm of the noble ones is itself the realm of sentient beings.

The inconceivable realm is the very mark of emptiness; it is devoid of sentient beings and free from all fetters and afflictions. Like space, it is formless, truly non-existent, untainted, and unattached. One knows that all sentient beings are entirely equal, neither emerging nor sinking, and that ultimate bodhi is free from the marks of sentient beings, just as the realm of space has nothing to be perceived.
Why is this? Because no dharma can be apprehended.
Such non-apprehension is precisely the characteristic of all dharmas and the characteristic of sentient beings; that which the mind perceives and realizes is itself not a realization.
Why is this? Because no dharma can be attained.
Such non-attainment is itself non-realization; therefore, it is called "attaining the stage of Anāgāmin."
"All sentient beings, all dharmas, and the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha—when such characteristics emerge, this is called an Anāgāmin.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"No longer returning, He has extinguished the dharmas of ordinary beings;”
Abandoning worldly conduct is called "Non-returner" (Anāgāmin).
Knowing there is no going or coming, no dwelling and no dependence;
having no fixed location, for this reason one does not return.
Having abandoned the state of ordinary beings, one becomes a Buddha’s protection;
never returning again is called *anāgāmin*.
Phenomena have no going, nor do they possess the characteristic of coming.
Neither coming nor going is called *anāgāmin*.
Having severed all craving and desire, and not being attached to the four kinds of nutriment;
not retreating from the site of enlightenment is called *anāgāmin*.
Having eliminated all sixty-two views,
yet having nowhere to go, he is called an Anāgāmin.
Detached from all existence, his mind is free from the mark of permanence.
Having realized things as they truly are, one does not come.
Nirvāṇa is quiescent and still, free from all afflictions;
having extinguished the marks of coming and going, one therefore does not come.
Having severed all evil destinies and abandoned every defilement, they realize nirvana; for this reason, they do not return.
They have utterly subdued their enemies and the generals of the demonic hosts.
Having transcended conventional designations, he therefore does not come.
Having extracted the arrow of ignorance and destroyed all craving;
having abandoned delight and desire, he therefore does not come.
Having extinguished all fetters and latent tendencies, he reveals the characteristics of the aggregates;
having attained definitive wisdom, he is named an Anāgāmin.
He has uprooted the thorns of sorrow and affliction and shattered the mountain of pride.
One who skillfully understands the five aggregates is called an Anāgāmin.
One who possesses ultimate illumination and adorns the Buddha-vehicle,
having emerged from the mire of desire, is called an Anāgāmin.
They fully know all hidden treasures and are supreme among those who possess them;
because they were established by the Buddha, they do not come here.
They abide securely in the most excellent, the unsurpassed Buddha-vehicle.
Having severed all fetters, one is called an Anāgāmin.
By means of the four great vows, one establishes bodhi;
having abided in bodhi, for this reason one does not return.
Knowing that all realms of space are inconceivable;
having eliminated all conceptualizations, they therefore do not come.
Regarding all sentient beings and the characteristics of the dharma-realm;
Because there is nothing to be attained, they do not come.
With a mind that grasps at nothing and does not follow after signs, they abide securely in bodhi; this is called an Anāgāmin.
The realm of sentient beings is empty and inconceivable;
knowing the Dharma to be thus, they therefore do not come.
In this way, Ānanda, the state of an Anāgāmin is revealed.
The various marks of non-obstruction establish the Buddha-dharma.
"Ānanda, you should know!
For the sake of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, the Tathāgata, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, has taught the state of an Anāgāmin through appropriate skillful means."
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"I shall now further explain the Arhat among Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.

Having extinguished all conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*) and cultivated the conduct of the Buddhas, they relinquish all that is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) while being able to bring all sentient beings to maturity and severing all their suffering and affliction; such a one is called an Arhat."
Not perceiving the mark of a sentient being, nor perceiving the mark of suffering and affliction—this is called an Arhat.

Having extinguished all grasping and attachment, abiding in the signless, knowing that all phenomena are empty, and being free from all marks such that nothing exists at all; having eliminated all the delusions, inversions, and ignorance of sentient beings, and thoroughly realized the inconceivable nature of the dharma of emptiness—this is the Arhat who attains inconceivable Bodhi. Because they have accomplished such dharmas, they are named Arhats.

Just as all Buddhas of the past have taught the Dharma that should be taught, so too shall all Buddhas of the future and present teach it; free from conceptual proliferation, fully pure and white, they proclaim the true Dharma of Bodhi—this is called an Arhat.
To establish sentient beings on the path to enlightenment without any grasping or attachment is called being an arhat.

One should practice the compassion of the various pāramitās; by attaining the great compassion of a Buddha, one fulfills the needs of sentient beings. This signless compassion can also establish all sentient beings. Thus, when practicing compassion without discrimination, not grasping at the notion of "sentient beings" nor the characteristic of "compassion," one is called an arhat.
To preach the Dharma for the sake of all sentient beings while grasping at nothing whatsoever among all phenomena—if one can act thus, one is called an Arhat.
To analytically demonstrate the faculties, powers, factors of enlightenment, and the path, remaining undefiled and unattached toward all sentient beings—one is called an Arhat.
One who thoroughly knows the mental activities of all sentient beings and gives rise to bodhicitta—one who can do so is called an arhat.
One who expounds upon all conditioned phenomena without grasping or attachment is called an arhat.
Furthermore, for the sake of all other sentient beings, they preach the practice of non-attachment and the practice of non-grasping; speaking in this way, they are called Arhats.
They travel through various Buddha-lands with minds free from the mark of going, arriving at the presence of every Buddha; perceiving them as Buddhas through signless wisdom, they are called Arhats.
If one can thus accomplish the Buddha-land and be fully endowed with all merits, it is also called the inconceivable, equal, stainless, and pure field of merit;
the field of merit of empty practice; the field of merit of non-retrogression (*avaivartika*);
the foremost pure field of merit devoid of the marks of women; and the field of merit free from all fetters (*saṃyojana*) and craving.
As the Buddha has realized and known: the field of merit that can exhaust all hindrances and obstructions; the field of merit that subdues all demons and defilements;
the field of merit that completely restrains the heterodox views of external paths; the field of merit of all [beings]; the field of merit of adornment;
the field of merit free from all fears; the field of merit of non-contention; and the field of merit of cessation.
The field of merit of supernormal powers, the most supreme field of merit, the field of merit that has no dwelling place, the inexhaustible field of merit,
the field of merit complete with the practices of Bodhisattvas, the most excellent field of merit of the Buddha’s sovereignty, the field of merit protected by the Buddhas,
and the field of merit of transformations— by means of these Dharma seals, [the Tathāgata] seals all sentient beings, causing them to...
They have attained the skillful exposition of the field of merit that brings peace and security;

they have attained the field of merit of the definitive nirvāṇa and cessation, adorned by all manner of jeweled ornaments within the Buddha-realm, and among all fields of merit, they have perfected such a field of merit.
One who is able to know that all phenomena are neither born nor extinguished is called an Arhat.
One who eliminates all defiled attachments and whose mind is not troubled even upon seeing those who come to provoke anger is called an Arhat.
One who does not grasp at the signs of any phenomena is called an Arhat.
One who eliminates the wisdom of habitual tendencies and cultivates supreme wisdom, thereby being able to realize it swiftly, is called an Arhat.
By means of these modes of deportment, one establishes awakening and the power of awakening; this is called an Arhat.

Such awakening is also called inconceivable, and that which is inconceivable is also called immovable. Being thus immovable, one is able to establish countless billions of kinds of sentient beings in awakening, free from all grasping and attachment, causing them all to abide in equanimity and be identical with the characteristic of dissolution and the characteristic of non-existence. Knowing that all dharmas enter into awakening, they abide in non-abiding—this is the Arhat.

Having known this, one is able to expound such a Dharma for the sake of sentient beings without becoming stained or attached; although there is verbal expression, there is no characteristic of speaking. One delivers all sentient beings, yet likewise does not grasp at the notion of "sentient beings. Regarding the two extremes of annihilationism and eternalism, one remains unmoved within the body; without severing afflictions, one is free from arrogance. Within all dharmas, there is non-arising, quiescence, and non-action; one does not destroy the characteristics of form, nor does one destroy the characteristics of the ordinary dharmas of sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, yet the mind remains unmoved.

Seeking liberation, one abides in the Buddha-dharma, yet this is not abiding in the liberation characterized by the fruit of a *srotāpanna*, nor in the liberation characterized by the fruits of a *sakṛdāgāmin*, an *anāgāmin*, or an *arhat*.
Liberation through the false view that all things arise from inversion; liberation through the false view of grasping at the wisdom of the Buddha;

liberation through the false view of grasping at the bodhicitta; liberation through the false view of practicing the giving of awakening; liberation through the false view of practicing the precepts of awakening;
liberation through the false view of patience toward harm and affliction; and liberation through the false view of diligence in the face of indolence.
Deluded views regarding the liberation of meditative concentration; deluded views regarding the liberation of wisdom through folly;
deluded views regarding the liberation of *śrāvakas* and ordinary worldlings; deluded views regarding parents, wives, children, and kinsmen—liberation from all such things as these;
and deluded views regarding the attachment to various desires and their immeasurable suffering.
From this, affection arises and defiled attachment is produced; these are the fetters and the source of affliction.
Within these phenomena, one gives rise to two kinds of marks; because one eliminates deluded thoughts and delivers sentient beings, one is called an Arhat.

To eliminate the delusive thoughts of craving for gain and offerings, as well as the distinction between the laity and those who have left home, one regards all things—from the most base and lowly to the most sublime dharmas—with complete equanimity.
Yet, one does not perceive these as mundane phenomena or those as Buddha-dharmas;
rather, to sever such delusive and inverted views, one teaches the Dharma of liberation. This is done if one wishes to adorn and purify a Buddha-field.
To bring such sentient beings to maturity through transformation is called nirvāṇa; such sentient beings are not called [attained to] nirvāṇa.
Such sentient beings are born into the various realms of existence (*bhava*); such sentient beings are not born into the various realms of existence.
Such sentient beings practice toward bodhi; such sentient beings do not practice toward bodhi. Thus...
Sentient beings violate the precepts; such sentient beings uphold the precepts;
such sentient beings are said to possess wisdom, while such sentient beings are said to lack wisdom;
for those sentient beings who give rise to dualistic thoughts and produce false imaginings, [the Buddha] acts to eliminate these states.
Conceptual construction is neither a field of merit nor a non-field of merit; it is that such beings practice with diligent vigor, and such beings do not practice with diligent vigor;
it is the dharma of the ignorant, the dharma of the wise, the dharma of women, the dharma of men, the dharma of the noble ones, and the dharma of those who are not noble—arising from...
Regarding these two conceptions: in order to eliminate such dualistic mental fabrications, the Bodhisattva dwells in neither non-retrogression from bodhi nor in retrogression from bodhi;
they have neither received the prediction of bodhi nor not received the prediction of bodhi;
they are neither near the seat of bodhi nor not near the seat of bodhi—such dualistic thoughts give rise to false conceptualizations.
In this way, although one attains bodhi and realizes bodhi, the bodhisattva does not obtain a truly real liberation from bodhi;
in short, attachment to all dharmas is entirely conceptual construction.
Therefore, Ānanda!

Because an Arhat is able to preach this markless Dharma (animitta-dharma) in order to sever the deluded thoughts of all sentient beings and enable them to attain liberation, such a person is called a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Arhat.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"Having eliminated all conditioned formations, And having departed from the cycle of birth and death;
Transcending the world—such a one is named an Arhat."
Having extinguished the fetters of affliction and delivered all suffering sentient beings, one is called an Arhat;
yet one perceives neither sentient beings nor any of the underlying tendencies.
Having no further benefit to seek in the dharmas, one is called an Arhat;
having extinguished deluded thoughts and dwelling in the state of non-delusion,
and knowing that all dharmas are empty, one is called an Arhat.
Knowing emptiness as supreme, one attains signlessness;
exhausting all signs is called an Arhat.
One extinguishes all evil signs of sentient beings.
Abandoning all signs is called being an arhat.
Having eliminated all extremes, one attains the state of non-conceptualization;
realizing this for oneself is called being an arhat.
For the sake of attaining bodhi, which is inconceivable,
they exert supreme diligence and are called arhats.
When they preach the Dharma, it is without fault or defilement.
Established in enlightenment, they are called Arhats;
as pure fields of merit, they cause all beings to attain happiness.
Not perceiving a "sentient being," they are called Arhats.
If one speaks of all dharmas, there is nothing at all to be grasped;
with neither dharma nor non-dharma, one is called an Arhat.
Having awakened to the roots and powers of the Path, they reveal them for the sake of the multitude.
Having attained the foremost fruit, he is named an Arhat.
Skillfully knowing sentient beings and purifying their bodhi, he explains these characteristics for them; thus he is called an Arhat.
Regarding all conditioned phenomena spoken of in the world,
one who is unattached to such formations is called an Arhat.
The World-Honored One is courageous, an inconceivable field of merit.
Following wherever the Buddha dwells, he expounds the Dharma for others.
If one wishes to see the Buddha, there is neither seeing nor not-seeing;
as the Buddha sees, so is one named an Arhat.
This is the field of merit, the field of merit of the noble sages;
possessing unsurpassed diligence, they are called Arhats.
Having distanced themselves from defiled desires, they do not harbor anger toward those who provoke it.
Furthermore, awakening is called arhatship.
Knowing that all phenomena are quiescent and signless,
for this reason awakening is named arhatship.
Unshaking all realms of sentient beings,
they cause countless billions to dwell securely in bodhi.
Both sentient beings and bodhi abide entirely in the signless.
Knowing that they are equal, one is called an Arhat;
attaining the peerless equality, one is identical with all dharmas;
and knowing the signless, one realizes the equality of bodhi.
One who can understand in this way is called an Arhat;
knowing the Dharma as it truly is, they are pure and free from turbidity.
They preach the Dharma for the sake of the multitude, yet there is nothing that is preached.
He delivers immeasurable multitudes, yet remains unshaken.
He perceives no sentient beings, nor the extremes of annihilation or permanence;
yet all beings see him deliver them from suffering and affliction.
Ultimate reality of all phenomena is without arising and without cessation;
yet through skillful means, one delivers and liberates sentient beings.
Without destroying form, feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness—it is likewise for these as well—this is precisely what is called liberation.
Toward all ordinary beings, they remain without signs of agitation;
they establish the Buddha-dharma and abide securely in liberation.
They are able to cause sentient beings not to dwell upon karmic retribution.
The Buddha’s mark of liberation is to preach the Dharma for others.
To falsely grasp at Bodhi while practicing giving,
or to maintain precepts and patience merely to eliminate delusive thoughts— [these are not true practice].
Laxity and indolence; striving for the grasping of signs—these are the marks of liberation removed by the Arhats' teaching.
To conceive thoughts of meditative concentration is the mark of the ignorant who lack wisdom.
To bring about liberation, he speaks of the Arhat.
This signless Dharma can eliminate all delusions;
preaching the Dharma in this way is what is called being an Arhat.
Sentient beings are deluded, grasping at the notion of śrāvakas;
yet there is no mark of liberation, for it is the Arhat who preaches the Dharma.
Parents, wives, and children—these are attachments born of ignorance.
This is not bodhi; it is attachment to birth and death.
To give rise to false affection for brothers and sisters, while regarding tranquil extinction and liberation as being an arhat—this is not bodhi.
Performing various karmic actions, they are greedily attached to those they hold dear;
upon seeing them, affection arises, thinking, "This was my relative from the start.
Thus they become mutually defiled by attachment, cherishing one another with intimacy.
Failing to recognize separation allows Māra to act with sovereignty;
not departing from the world is the ultimate evil—
such are the afflictions as spoken by the Arhats.
Regarding all fetters and latent tendencies, he has fully awakened;
both are empty and false, as taught by the Arhat.
For the benefit of many people, he practices without conceptual proliferation.
Such is liberation, as taught by the Arhats.
Whether lay or ordained, most give rise to delusive thoughts;
the ignorant grasp and cling, while the Arhats are liberated.
Seeing the fetters of the household, he extensively reveals the True Dharma;
while the ignorant and foolish harbor deluded thoughts, the Arhat attains liberation.
Abandoning the state of an ordinary person brings no benefit to the Buddha-dharma.
Abandoning both gain and loss is called being an Arhat.
Seeing distinctions such as high and low, or various other kinds, sentient beings grasp at mental conceptions; the Arhat is liberated from these.
Accomplishing the grasping of signs, one practices extensively;
thus, through attachment to signs, one is well able to attain liberation.
Attaining the Buddha-field of merit, one reaches ultimate reality.
False grasping is the field; the Arhat is liberated.
There is neither extinction nor non-extinction, neither a thing nor a non-thing;
though one cultivates bodhi, one does not attain bodhi.
Observing the precepts or violating them, possessing wisdom or lacking it—
sentient beings, in their ignorance, give rise to these dualistic conceptions.
People mostly engage in grasping and attachment, which manifests in many various forms.
Liberation from these perceptions is what the Arhats have taught.
To perceive a field of merit where there is no field of merit,
or for the ignorant and foolish to form various perceptions— these are but delusions.
Toward all women and men, and toward the dharmas of the noble and the non-noble, they give rise to two kinds of thoughts.
Such beings are ordinary, foolish, and without wisdom.
Grasping at the two notions, the Arhat attains liberation.
Regarding the dharmas of falling back or not falling back, and the determinate or indeterminate;
sitting near enlightenment, yet not grasping at enlightenment.
Having attained bodhi, one reaches ultimate quiescence;
forever departing from birth and death, one conceives the thought of nirvana.
One severs the bonds of sentient beings and extinguishes all marks.
Therefore, the Arhat is known as "liberation by name.
It is the nature of things for a Bodhisattva to manifest as an Arhat;
when they attain the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena, that itself is the wisdom of an Arhat.
"An Arhat such as this is not disparaged by Bodhisattvas;
their minds always abide in supreme bodhi.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Ānanda, saying:
"You should now know!
This is what the Tathāgata, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, has provisionally taught as 'arhat' for the sake of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. Ānanda said:
“How is it that the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, further designates bodhisattva-mahāsattvas as ‘śrāvakas’? The Buddha said, “Ānanda!
A Bodhisattva can cause immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* sentient beings to hear all things through the sound of the Buddha-dharma; therefore, they are called *śrāvakas*.

Furthermore, they cause them to hear inconceivable sounds; having heard these inconceivable sounds, they become free from conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) regarding bodhi. Because they cause others to hear through pure sounds, they are also called *śrāvakas*.
Furthermore, they cause others to hear that only the bliss of nirvana exists and no other bliss; hearing such sounds is also called being a śrāvaka.

Moreover, they cause others to hear of the faculties, powers, factors of enlightenment, the path, meditative concentrations, liberations, various samādhis, and the foundations of mindfulness and right efforts that realize the state of no-remainder; causing countless multitudes to hear all such teachings is also called being a śrāvaka.

This body is suffering, empty, and without self; yet the characteristics of all the aggregates (skandhas) are unattainable. Foolish ordinary beings, through their ignorance, conceptually differentiate this body and give rise to false grasping and attachment; hearing such sounds as these, they are also called śrāvakas.

Furthermore, one realizes that the eye-element is false and unreal; even up to the Buddha-eye, all are identical to the eye-element and inconceivable. It can cause sentient beings to see things as they truly are. Regarding all phenomena, there is no characteristic of accomplishment; this is called the "accomplished eye. Such a dharma-characteristic causes sentient beings to hear its name, and thus they are called "Hearers" (śrāvaka).

Just as an echo is made to be heard by sentient beings and is thus called "voice-hearer" (śrāvaka), one should not falsely grasp or become attached to sound. Since there is no characteristic of sound and nothing to be attained, hearing such a sound is what is meant by being a voice-hearer.

One should not grasp at the characteristics of fragrance within fragrance, nor is anything to be found therein. For example, it is like a person who, in a dream, smells a fragrance; although there is truly no fragrance, they falsely give rise to the perception of fragrance within that which is fragranceless. This is merely a delusion arising from one’s own conceptualization, yet the foolish and ignorant accept and grasp at these characteristics of fragrance. Hearing such sounds, they are called "Śrāvakas" (Hearers).

The characteristic of the tongue-faculty (*jihvā-āyatana*) is empty; it is like a piece of flesh that cannot perceive taste, and like a mass of foam, for which no further analogy can be found, as it transcends all metaphors. It is neither taste nor a faculty. When one analyzes the characteristic of taste, nothing at all is found. Thus, the realm of taste (*rasa-dhātu*) and the inconceivable realm are equal and non-dual. Free from mind and thought, and devoid of deliberation, there is truly no mental perception. One who hears such sounds is called a *śrāvaka*.
Those who cause others to hear all the dharmas they have already realized are called śrāvakas.

If, upon hearing, one discerns the characteristics of the body, realizing that the essence of these bodily characteristics is fundamentally empty—neither arising nor non-arising—this is called bodhi; to cause immeasurable multitudes to hear this sound is called being a śrāvaka.

The nature of the mind has no substance and truly exists as nothing; it is entirely like an illusion or a magical transformation, neither arising nor ceasing. Because it enables all sentient beings to hear its name, it is called "hearing" (śrāvaka).
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"The Dharma-giving of the śrāvakas is inconceivable; attaining realization of this path is called 'inconceivable,' and it is by means of this inconceivable Dharma-giving that bodhi can be generated."
Why is this? Because it arises from seeds that are similar [to their cause].
Taking what is not a fruit as a fruit is not obtained through the giving of material wealth; because one hears, believes, and understands [the Dharma], one is called a Śrāvaka (Hearer).

Material giving is minor; the gift of Dharma is supreme. Such a gift of Dharma does not harbor envy toward others, nor does it possess the mark of giving, nor is it attached to that giving. It is like a magical illusion, free from discrimination; it gives rise to no aspirations and does not grasp at the notion of giving, because it is devoid of longing.
Ānanda, you should know that such a donor accomplishes bodhi; because they hear, believe, and understand, they are called śrāvakas.
Exhausting all marks and severing all fetters and afflictions, they surpass the entire assembly of śrāvakas and proclaim the Buddha-dharma with a great voice.
Why is this? Because they have attained the perfection of sound that transcends all other sounds.

Having produced this sound, they cause others to hear the Buddha-dharma; they understand that the characteristics of all sounds are neither identical nor different, thereby achieving right faith. They teach the Dharma as being neither dual nor non-dual. Those who hear such a teaching are called Śrāvakas.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"Immeasurable sentient beings hear The inconceivable Buddha-dharma;
The vast eloquence of the Bodhisattvas— This is what is called a Śrāvaka."
Having heard [the Dharma], they believe in Bodhi, free from turbidity and conceptual proliferation;
causing all to hear it—these are called Śrāvakas.
Having heard of the bliss of Nirvāṇa, this bliss is the most supreme.
Causing all to hear of quiescent extinction—this is called a śrāvaka.
The various powers and the factors of enlightenment, The foundations of mindfulness, the faculties, and so forth;
Swiftly attaining the ultimate goal—this is called a śrāvaka.
Hearing that this body is suffering and empty, Lacking any mark of solidity or substance;
That it is invaded by greed, hatred, and delusion— For these reasons, one discriminates the body.
One also hears regarding the eye-base: It is not real, yet one perceives it as real.
Sentient beings are largely deluded; ordinary folk are blind and lack wisdom.
If they obtain the Buddha-eye, they will see the inconceivable with right view.
Having attained such an eye, they will no longer possess any delusions.
All dharmas are without attainment, yet all sentient beings hear them;
by such causes and conditions, they are also called Śrāvakas.
The characteristics of all dharmas are like the echo of a call.
In this, there is no one who hears, nor is there anyone who speaks;
yet causing countless multitudes to hear—this is called a Śrāvaka (Hearer).
In this, there is nothing heard, and there is no one who is stained by attachment.
For example, as when a person in a dream, though they may smell many kinds of fragrances, not a single one is truly established; thus should one know the nature of fragrance.
Being free from all defilements, there is likewise no one who smells the fragrance.
The liberation of the Bodhisattva is for the sake of the many deluded sentient beings.
Hearing that the tongue is like a piece of meat, they are unable to know its flavor;
if a piece of meat could know flavor, it too would surely know equality.
Discerning such characteristics, one knows that craving for flavors is the most evil;
this realm is inconceivable—this is called knowing flavors.
Having definitively known flavors, the Bodhisattva remains unattached.
Causing the assembly to hear with certainty—this is called a śrāvaka.
Contemplating the body’s differentiated marks, its fundamental nature is empty and unarisen;
if one knows this reality, there is neither arising nor that which can cause it to arise.
Such is the nature of Bodhi: it neither arises nor can it give rise [to anything].
To cause all sentient beings to hear this universally is what is called being a Śrāvaka.
One should likewise know that the mind is such: its essential nature is non-existent.
Because emptiness has no intrinsic nature, it enables all to hear.
Just as the dharmas of things are unarisen, unceasing, and non-dual;
being signless and without anything seen—this is called a śrāvaka.
May all hear of this giving—this inconceivable gift of Dharma;
may they practice and proceed to the site of enlightenment, achieving Bodhi.
Just as various kinds of seeds each yield their corresponding fruits, so too shall it be.
Cultivating inconceivable generosity, the realization of the Way is likewise so.
Giving away all material wealth, the gift of Dharma is supreme;
a mind of relinquishment free from greed and envy—this is called the path to Bodhi.
The mind is always free from attachment; though one gives, there is no dependence.
If one can give in this manner, one will swiftly realize Bodhi.
Being able to leave all marks behind and completely relinquish all fetters and afflictions—
Free from all defilements and attachments, such a one is called a śrāvaka.
Their voice is most subtle and exquisite, the supreme among all sounds;
this voice is heard afar, proclaiming the inconceivable Dharma of the Buddha.
Able to cause all to know that all sounds have no basis;
Neither one nor different—this is called a śrāvaka.
Wishing to cause all to hear what the Buddhas have spoken;
According to the sounds of the Dharma they hear, all give rise to the aspiration for enlightenment (*bodhicitta*).
Among all fields of merit, they hear that the Buddha-field is the most supreme;
wherever the Buddha dwells, they draw near to the World-Savior.
Let it be heard throughout the three thousandfold world-system, abiding peacefully in empty space;
so too it is with all sentient beings—they are all identical to the mark of nirvāṇa.
The four great elements that have been taught were analyzed for the sake of sentient beings.
Just like the characteristics of space, they are equal to the inconceivable.
Such are the characteristics of all realms; there is likewise no one who can know them.
Within them there is neither birth-and-death, nor affliction, nor nirvana.
All phenomena lack true reality, and sentient beings are likewise so;
this is called the realm of quiescence—how could one perceive a being?
For the sake of immeasurable sentient beings, may they constantly hear and know this day and night.
Not attached to their own fame or profit, they preach only for the sake of sentient beings.
You should know that these are śrāvakas who desire to let all hear;
though it is not actually the dharma of śrāvakas, they merely manifest as śrāvakas.
The Hero of the World speaks by means of provisional names; he is the most supreme among those who preach the Dharma.
Therefore, know that all sentient beings are entirely of the nature of suchness.
These are called śrāvakas, who are free from outflows and have severed their fetters.
Liberated from all fetters, he speaks for the sake of sentient beings;
manifesting freedom from all bonds, pure and without frivolity;
having seen this, he speaks of it for others—the Buddha-dharma is likewise in every respect.
Before long they shall behold that which is taught by the Buddha;
the practice cultivated by Bodhisattvas, wherein there is no attachment to phenomena.
These are called Śrāvakas, untethered and pure.
I also cause all to hear it, so that they may practice according to what they have heard.
Ānanda, you should know: these are taught by me through skillful means;
thus should one understand the śrāvakas, for the bodhisattva has no basis of reliance.
“Ānanda, you should know!
This is what the Tathāgata, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, calls ‘śrāvakas’ as a skillful means for the sake of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. Ānanda said:
“How does the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha further teach the Dharma of the Pratyekabuddhas to the Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas? The Buddha said, “Ānanda!
The Bodhisattva directly perceives all phenomena.
How does he perceive them?

It means that he knows all phenomena are without contention and are merely provisional designations; without destroying the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), he is able to see and realize phenomena—this is called a Pratyekabuddha.

The Buddha is inconceivable; regarding all phenomena and all sentient beings, he is identical to the mark of nirvāṇa, without distinction. He is formless, signless, pure, and quiescent. The limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), the limit of sentient beings, and the limit of nirvāṇa are like shadows and illusions—without boundaries and non-existent. Within these limits, there is no characteristic of a limit; they are beyond speech and description, without basis and without that which can be described.

Why is this? Just as I know that emptiness is without arising and without cessation, and thus know the limit of sentient beings, so too do I know that the limit of phenomena and the limit of birth-and-death are themselves the limit of the Buddha. To know such limits is called a Pratyekabuddha.

Presently one knows form; that which is form is called the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*). Once the aggregate of form has been exhausted, there remains only conventional expression, devoid of self or what belongs to a self. Why is this so?

As it is said regarding the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*), it exists only as a verbal expression; it is empty, without arising, and without ceasing. Since speech itself lacks the characteristics of speech, how can one speak?

To speak of this aggregate of form is likewise to perceive directly that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—even up to speaking of the aggregate of consciousness—should be known as the provisional designation "aggregate of consciousness" and so forth, existing only as verbal expressions.
All such expressions are empty, without arising, and without ceasing; they are neither real nor unreal.

If even verbal expression does not exist, how much less so the characteristics of the aggregates? Thus, these five aggregates arise from conventional designations; this is called a pratyekabuddha. Why is this?

Because of names and verbal expressions, one speaks of "form" (*rūpa*); yet form is merely a provisional name, having neither cause nor non-cause, though it is designated as a "cause. These causal conditions of the aggregates (*skandha*) have an ineffable character; all phenomena are without support and without conditions. To awaken to and know this is what is called a *pratyekabuddha*.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"Directly perceiving all phenomena, One knows them all to be without contention;
Neither arising nor decaying, They possess no mark of turbidity or disorder."
Directly perceiving all phenomena, their intrinsic nature is entirely empty and quiescent;
since their essence and characteristics are thus, there is nothing that is fixed.
Directly perceiving the ultimate state, all phenomena are likewise so.
This is called right knowledge; the Pratyekabuddha is inconceivable.
Sentient beings and nirvāṇa—no prior limit can be found for them.
This limit is without arising; even the Buddha is difficult to conceive.
Just as the nirvāṇa of sentient beings has neither arising nor a place of departure;
if a phenomenon lacks the characteristic of arising, this is called nirvāṇa.
Sentient beings and nirvāṇa are both like reflections in water.
There are appearances but no sentient beings; this is called nirvāṇa.
Sentient beings and nirvāṇa are all spoken of as mere conventional designations;
there is neither arising nor ceasing, but only provisional names.
Regarding such characteristics of verbal expression, one knows that no sentient beings exist;
this meaning should be understood: sentient beings are themselves nirvāṇa.
All verbal expressions are empty; there is neither mind nor phenomena.
Using speech to express what is beyond speech, there is ultimately no one who knows it.
The limit of non-speech is without support, and speech likewise has no abiding place;
such is the nature of speech, inconceivable to sentient beings.
Sentient beings and nirvāṇa, the reality-limit and the non-reality-limit;
Transcending them, one attains peace and security, forever proceeding toward the abode of quiescence.
The limit of all sentient beings is like a shadow or an echo.
Without cause and without condition, the reality-limit (bhūtakoṭi) is inconceivable.
The source of all dharmas is expressed only by provisional names;
this limit is non-existent and cannot be grasped through the characteristics of names.
The ultimate reality (bhūtakoṭi) is beyond verbal expression, and there is no one who can know it;
because emptiness is itself the ultimate reality, sentient beings are inconceivable.
The ultimate reality is beyond verbal expression, yet verbal expression achieves nothing therein.
The true mark is suchness, and sentient beings are likewise boundless.
The marks of verbal expression are empty by nature; they are not known through words alone.
As you have described it, sentient beings are unable to conceive of it.
Such is the characteristic of the reality-limit (bhūtakoṭi), which cannot be known through thought or deliberation;
this is called the teaching of the Perfectly Awakened One, difficult for even a Pratyekabuddha to conceive.
When one directly perceives the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha), there is only a provisional name.
Such is the nature of the characteristics of the aggregates (*skandha*): they are eternally beyond verbal expression.
Lacking any mark of reality, this is called "transcending the world.
Knowing the aggregates in this way, one realizes their fundamental nature has no place of abiding.
This form is non-existent; it is merely designated as an aggregate (skandha).
It is but an empty name, neither arising nor ceasing.
Words and all phenomena have no fixed location.
If there were no verbal designations, it would be called the "aggregate of form.
As for the aggregate of sensation, perception, mental formations,
and likewise up to the aggregate of consciousness— all these exist only as conventional verbal designations.
The aggregates are seen as ineffable, detached from all marks;
their intrinsic nature is non-existent, neither arising nor abiding.
As this reality has been taught, it is far removed from all phenomena.
Knowing all such marks in this way, their essential nature has no place of abiding.
They are spoken of by means of provisional names; even the explanation of the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth is empty.
Having known that verbal expression is empty, there is neither arising nor ceasing.
Discourse and all phenomena have no fixed location;
if there were no discourse, that would be called the aggregate of consciousness.
This aggregate is beyond discourse and cannot be measured.
Without the characteristics of arising or ceasing, and likewise having no place of dependence;
liberated from all afflictions, it is neither karma nor its retribution;
it is neither awakening nor the aggregates, neither speech nor nirvana.
This perception is without certainty, nor is there any wisdom;
it is unattainable internally or externally, and there is neither indolence nor diligence.
There is no frivolity or doubt, nor is there any accomplishment.
Neither startled nor terrified, there is no such thing as form at all.
One does not perceive emptiness, and the signless is likewise so;
there are no characteristics of unity or difference, neither bound nor liberated.
All words and sounds—this voice enters into nothing;
this is called *Ruta*, which cannot be reached by speech.
Having reached the ultimate in direct perception, he proclaims the inexhaustible Dharma.
Having attained this samādhi, one does not cling to verbal expression.
If this wisdom is directly perceived, it is described as equal to *aruta*;
since *ruta* is identical to all phenomena, it is expounded through silence.
In this direct perception of the inversion, there is no dependence on other causes and conditions;
this is called Perfect Enlightenment, the inconceivable state of the Pratyekabuddha.
