Chapter Four: A Further Explanation of the Characteristics of the Two Vehicles “Ānanda! Thus, a bodhisattva-mahāsattva clearly knows ignorance and non-ignorance;

he knows formations and non-formations; he knows consciousness and the characteristics of consciousness; he knows name-and-form and the characteristics of name-and-form; he knows the six sense bases and the characteristics of the six sense bases; he knows contact and the characteristics of contact; he knows feeling and the characteristics of feeling; he knows craving and the characteristics of craving; he knows grasping and the characteristics of grasping; he knows becoming and the characteristics of becoming; he knows birth and the characteristics of birth; and he knows old age and death and the characteristics of old age and death. By cultivating and realizing these through direct perception, he is called a pratyekabuddha.”
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"Manifestly seeing ignorance, yet having nothing known;
There is no accomplishment, like a reflection in water."
Wisdom is also immovable and does not cling to phenomena;
if one does not cling to phenomena, this is called the mark of wisdom.
Ignorance is like space, which is the characteristic of all phenomena.
Arriving at direct perception, this is called a Pratyekabuddha.
If one speaks of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), they are neither internal nor external;
nor do they arise from a Buddha, yet they give rise to conditioned activity.
These practices are merely provisional names; they are definitively non-existent.
Without arising and without ceasing, they are like empty space.
Upon reaching this direct realization, the bodhisattva is fearless.
This is called perfect enlightenment; the realization of the Pratyekabuddhas is inconceivable.
To know that all phenomena are like illusions and transformations, and having clearly understood them as such, is what is called "direct vision."
Not knowing things as they truly are is the sphere of activity of consciousness;

this conceptualization is discrimination. Knowing that the phenomena of consciousness are empty, one realizes that consciousness and wisdom are not distinct from wisdom, and thus remains unattached to anything at all.
If one knows that regarding phenomena, consciousness is like an illusion;
that name-and-form arise through causes and conditions and possess the marks of the conditioned;
they have no definitive essence, nor are they established.
Detached from the six sense bases, yet one speaks of the characteristics of the six sense bases;
these verbal expressions and sounds are all empty in their essential nature.
Contact arises from the six sense bases, being devoid of causal conditions.
Discrimination is contact; like an illusion, it is entirely empty.
This contact has no substance; it arises from deluded thought.
Contact has no reality, nor does it have a place of abiding.
Directly perceiving contact, one knows it has no characteristic of contact;
having accomplished weary detachment, such a one is called a Pratyekabuddha.
If one realizes that feeling is as unsubstantial as a bubble;
Both nature and characteristics are empty; ultimately, they possess no reality.
Severing the fetters of craving, one attains the state of non-craving;
having brought all desires to an end, this is called a Pratyekabuddha.
Discrimination regarding grasping is empty and non-existent;
like a mirage in the heat, it has no accomplishment.
There is no notion of action, and the notion of arising is likewise.
Knowing the nature of birth is empty, quiescent, and non-existent;
one attains freedom from old age and likewise fears not death;
having nothing further to achieve, one does not undergo future existence.
"Beholding these dharmas as they truly are, one finds nothing upon which to rely;
yet through the voice of an awakened one, one practices as a bodhisattva in reality. Ānanda!"
"You should now know that these Tathāgatas, the Samyaksaṃbuddhas, have skillfully taught the Pratyekabuddhas for the sake of the Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
At that time, Ānanda rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and spoke in verse:
"Nirvāṇa is not nirvāṇa; It delivers the world."
Just as a knot in space is untied by means of space itself,
so too, if one can speak in this way, it is called "having something to say.
The World-Honored One, through skillful means, speaks the Dharma of non-attachment.
At that time, after Ānanda had spoken these verses, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
All those in the world are shrouded by ignorance and thus deceive themselves; they do not understand that the Tathāgata speaks through the use of provisional names.”

The dharmas of those who practice through faith and those who practice through the Dharma, the eight types of noble persons, and the stages of srotāpanna, sakṛdāgāmin, anāgāmin, arhat, śrāvaka, and pratyekabuddha.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Ānanda:

"In the past, you did not forget provisional names under the Buddhas and planted various roots of goodness; because you have skillfully understood provisional names, you have not been plundered by ignorance and darkness."
Why is this? All dharmas are mere provisional designations, like an illusion, like a reflection in water, like a mirage in the heat, like an echo.
Such are these provisional designations, Ānanda!

You should now know that you shall not be harmed by any evils; you shall adorn yourself with complete and perfect adornments; you shall be able to understand that all phenomena are merely provisional names arising from causes and conditions; you shall achieve diligence without any forgetfulness, yet without grasping at the mark of diligence; you shall be without forgetfulness, attaining the most supreme wisdom, yet without grasping at the mark of wisdom.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
“Foolish sentient beings, Lax and lacking wisdom, Do not understand conventional designations; They ought to apply themselves with diligent vigor.”
Able to resolve conventional designations, Knowing the aggregates as they truly are;
Rescuing and delivering the world, Causing it to attain true wisdom.
Having known that conventional designations are empty, One immediately awakens to Bodhi.
Nor is awakening attained; this is what is called the teaching of awakening.
Provisional names are themselves the mark of emptiness; emptiness cannot know emptiness.
Emptiness is but a sound, free from all contentious debate.
To manifest such a meaning: in emptiness there is nothing to be grasped;
nor is there any place where realization can be found. How, then, could there be one who attains?
This is called the "emptiness of emptiness."
"Thus it is, Ānanda!

You should know that the dharma of emptiness is profoundly deep and immeasurable; one should not give rise to negligence, nor shall there be any loss. This is called the exposition of the stage of perfected practice for a pratyekabuddha."

At that time, there were five billion bhikṣus within the assembly who had all attained the stage of faith-practice (śraddhācaryā). They rose from their seats and, standing before the World-Honored One, spoke these verses in unison:
"Having abandoned doubt and attained right wisdom, O Supreme Lord, Savior of the World;
The World-Honored One speaks of provisional names, And those of faith-practice abide in Bodhi."

At that time, there were another five billion bhikṣus practicing the Dharma within the assembly. Having heard these verses, they rose from their seats, adjusted their robes, and together spoke in verse:
"We have removed our doubts through the illumination of Bodhi;
The Tathāgata has taught the provisional dharmas, And those who practice the Dharma abide in Bodhi."

At that time, there were another ten billion bhikṣus of the eight classes within the assembly. Having heard these verses, they rose from their seats, stood before the Buddha, and together spoke in verse:
"We have long since abandoned doubt and regret, Having practiced for a long time as those of the eight classes;
The Tathāgata speaks of them as provisional names, Yet the eight classes abide in Bodhi."

At that time, there were another ten billion stream-enterers (*srotāpanna*) within the assembly who, having heard these verses, rose from their seats and stood before the Buddha, speaking these verses in unison:
“Now we have received illumination From the Holy Lord, Savior of the World;
We understand the Dharma taught by the Buddha, Which reveals the nature of provisional designations.”

At that time, there were another two million five hundred thousand *srotāpanna* bhikṣus in the assembly who, having heard these verses, rose from their seats, stood before the Buddha, and together spoke these verses:
“Formerly we had attachments, And thus attained the stage of *srotāpanna*;
Now, free from all delusive thoughts, We are tranquil and beyond conceptual proliferation.”
At that time, there were another ten billion *anāgāmins* within the assembly who, having heard these verses, rose from their seats and stood before the Buddha, speaking these verses in unison:
“O Unsurpassed Honored One, Savior of the World, You have caused us to leave behind conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*);
Having uprooted the notion of fruition, You illuminate the path to Bodhi.”

At that time, there were another thirty-five billion bhikṣus within the assembly, all of whom dwelt in the four dhyānas and had attained arhatship. Having heard the recitation of the verse, they rose from their seats, stood before the Buddha, and together spoke these verses:
"We have now attained freedom from defilement, Realizing for ourselves the state of nirvana without remainder;
All vehicles enter the One Vehicle, Like an illusion, without fixed determination."
At that time, there were another twenty thousand bhikṣus in the assembly who, having heard these verses, rose from their seats, stood before the Buddha, and together spoke these verses:
"We formerly clung to false speech; The World-Honored One has taught them as mere designations.
We called ourselves śrāvakas, Abiding in dharmas that are but designations."

At that time, there were another five thousand bhikṣus within the assembly who were established in the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas. Having heard these verses, they rose from their seats, stood before the Buddha, and together spoke these verses:
“We have now attained direct vision Of the awakening of a pratyekabuddha;
The Tathāgata speaks of it as a provisional name, Yet the awakening of a pratyekabuddha is inconceivable.”

At that time, there were another one million bhikṣuṇīs within the assembly who conceived the notion that they had attained the fruits of srotāpanna, sakṛdāgāmin, anāgāmin, and arhat. Having heard the recitation of the verse, they rose from their seats, stood before the Buddha, and together spoke these verses:
“May we, within this female form, All enter into the Dharma of equality;
The World-Honored One’s teaching is without distinction, His illumination is supreme.”

At that time, there were also eight million *upāsakas* and *upāsikās* within the assembly who all considered themselves to have attained the fruits of *srotāpanna*, *sakṛdāgāmin*, *anāgāmin*, and *arhat*. Having heard these verses, they rose from their seats, stood before the Buddha, and spoke these verses:
"Now our minds are free from defilement, Pure as lapis lazuli;
Only now do we truly call ourselves renunciants, Having attained abiding in the Buddha-dharma."
At that time, there were sixty billion nayutas of devas in the void who scattered celestial māndārava flowers over the Buddha. Before the Tathāgata, they spoke these verses in unison:
"Previously, we conceived the notion of vehicles And were greedily attached to various fruits;
Now we have completely abandoned them all, And have finally awakened to the path of bodhi."

Chapter Five: Eliminating Conceptions. From the *Anuttara-dharma-paryāya-sūtra*, Chapter Five, "Eliminating Conceptions. At that time, there were among the assembly immeasurable hundreds of thousands of arhats, with Śāriputra, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Subhūti, Aniruddha, Anuruddha, Kapphiṇa, and Gavāmpati as their leaders. They rose from their seats, adjusted their robes, stood before the World-Honored One, bowed respectfully, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"

I now make this true vow: may those who are free from delusive thoughts yet subdue the various māras; who are fully possessed of the five heinous crimes, fully possessed of the five desires, and fully possessed of false views; who have abandoned right view and have severed the lives of immeasurable sentient beings—may I now cause them all to attain bodhi and enter nirvana without remainder.
At that time, the World-Honored One remained silent.
The assembly of immeasurable hundreds of thousands of people in the gathering all gave rise to doubt and wonder:
"For what reason is this so?"
"Now we are all utterly blind and ignorant, lacking any realization; yet even the Arhats speak thus—how much more so the ordinary worldlings?
Each sat in one place without moving, and none of those sitting could rise, nor could any who were standing sit down.
They all said, "Why do you speak in such a manner?"

At that time, Ānanda, for the sake of the great assembly of hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of sentient beings, by means of the Buddha’s spiritual power, came to know his own mind and the minds of others, and asked Mañjuśrī:

“This great assembly, numbering hundreds of thousands of millions and so forth, having heard these words spoken by the Arhats, has all given rise to doubt and confusion. I pray only that Mañjuśrī will analyze and explain their causes and conditions for me.”
At that time, the Tathāgata remained silent.
Mañjuśrī addressed Ānanda, saying:
"This bodhisattva of the stage of non-retrogression has made such a statement for the sake of the karmic conditions involving these great virtuous ones."
Ānanda said: “Mañjuśrī! Is the stage of non-retrogression bodhi?”
Mañjuśrī replied: "So it is, so it is!
This stage of non-retrogression is the bodhi of all these venerable ones."
Ānanda asked, "Venerable ones, for what reason do you speak thus?
At that time, Mañjuśrī said to Ānanda:
“With ignorance as mother, craving arises from volitional formations; by bringing these to ultimate extinction, one completely eliminates all enmity and harm.
With perverted perceptions as father, by departing from inversion and extinguishing desire and craving, one becomes an Arhat—firm, unbreakable, and indestructible.

One exhausts the notion of being an ordinary person as well as the notion of being a member of the Saṃgha; because these notions are destroyed, one is able to cultivate the notion of all dharmas as indestructible, even to the point of not grasping at the notion of a Tathāgata, training in non-arising and ultimately attaining eternal detachment.”
"Venerable Ānanda!
The various elders have spoken thus:
'How is it that I am now fully possessed of the five heinous crimes?'"
"Why is this? Because there is neither thought of coming nor thought of going; for this reason, it is called being fully possessed of the five heinous crimes.
Furthermore, Ānanda said:
"What are the five desires?
These bhikṣus understand the five desires to be like a dream, like an illusion, like bubbles on water, and like an echo; thus they are fully endowed with wisdom.
How is it that wisdom is complete, neither increasing nor decreasing?
How is it that the five desires are likewise neither increasing nor decreasing?
For what reason?

Having realized, in accordance with reality, that these five desires are ultimately without substance and without characteristics, one attains the wisdom that perceives the true nature of the five desires; therefore, this is called being "fully endowed with the five desires."
For this reason, the Venerable Ones have made this statement:
"I now possess the five objects of desire. Ānanda!
What is the possession of wrong view and the departure from right view?
To grasp at and cling to all phenomena is called wrong view;
wrong view is a false conceptualization. All phenomena have neither support nor lack support; they are like space, having no refuge and no basis.
Why is this? Because no real entity can be found among all phenomena; one should know them in this way.
All phenomena are entirely equal; to eliminate even the notion of equality is called right view.
Why is this? Such perceptions as these are themselves evil perceptions.
For this reason, O venerable bhikṣus, one perceives neither equal perceptions nor evil perceptions.
Why is this? Because the exhaustion of all conceptualizations is called the Bodhi of the Buddha.
Having attained Bodhi, one does not perceive even the slightest dharma that can be apprehended.
Ānanda! For this reason, the bhikṣu of great virtue spoke thus:
"One who is separated from right view is fully possessed of wrong view."
"Ānanda! For what reason do these bhikṣus say:
'We have now truly taken the lives of hundreds of thousands of sentient beings'?"

When the Great Virtuous Ones uttered these words, hundreds of thousands of millions of devas, hearing such an exposition, immediately attained the realization that all phenomena are like dreams, like illusions, like reflections in water, and like echoes. Having attained this realization, they severed their notions of sentient beings, persons, life-span, and individuals. They also immediately attained liberation from the seeds [of existence], and regarding the roots of merit for bodhi and all phenomena, they realized there was no arising, no activity, and nothing to be cultivated. Hearing the teaching on conventional designations, they believed deeply without doubt; likewise, the upāsakas and upāsikās all completely severed their notions of sentient beings, persons, life-span, and individuals.
Having eliminated these perceptions, one no longer undergoes birth again and again. Why is this?

Because by severing the notions of a sentient being (*sattva*), a person (*pudgala*), a life-force (*jīva*), a human (*manuja*), and a hungry ghost (*preta*), one is subject to repeated births and deaths due to the presence of such notions; once these notions are abandoned, one attains the ultimate self-realization of non-arising (*anutpāda*).
For this reason, O Venerable Ones!

By such skillful means, one speaks of conventional designations, saying that one has severed the lives of immeasurable sentient beings; therefore, it is said that one fully attains the Bodhi of a Buddha.

I shall now enter parinirvāṇa in the nirvana without remainder; having attained the marks and signs of a Buddha, I shall thereby teach and transform immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of sentient beings, extinguishing all fetters and afflictions just as the Buddha has realized.

Why is this? It is so that all sentient beings may give rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and having attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), they may attain *bodhi*. Furthermore, they do not abandon afflictions (*kleśa*) nor do they approach the Buddha-dharma; rather, the afflictions born of their own minds are extinguished without remainder.
For this reason, all the venerable ones said:
"I have now attained bodhi. Ānanda!
Therefore, it is now called "non-arising. Why is this?

Because such sons and daughters of good family, having resolved their minds toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, illuminate all phenomena; yet once they have resolved their minds toward *bodhi*, there is nothing to be attained. Being free from the marks of *bodhi* and the marks of all phenomena, they enter *parinirvāṇa* in *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*.

Ānanda! Thus, when men and women of good family who have set out upon the Bodhisattva vehicle do not conceive the notion of day by seeing the sun, whereas ordinary, foolish people, upon seeing the sun, immediately form the notion of day—they are not wise ones.
Why is this so? Ānanda!
If the sun possessed a substantial body that was not illusory, it could be accumulated; however, because it is illusory, it has neither past nor future, and the same applies to the night.
If one perceives day as the thought of day and night as the thought of night, this is what is seen through the deluded imaginings of ordinary fools. Ānanda!

For those of the Bodhisattva vehicle who practice for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and have a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*), they should not give rise to the thought of day during the day, nor give rise to the thought of night at night.
"Why is this? Because by being free from all conceptualizations, one can abide in the path of the Tathāgata’s bodhi.
At that time, Mañjuśrī spoke these verses:
“Ignorance is the mother, born from the formations;
if one cuts its root, this is called the destruction of harm.
Craving and various perverted perceptions—these are said to be the father.”
If one can know things as they truly are, Ultimately there is nothing at all.
Knowing that all are entirely illusory, One then cuts off all roots;
Without conditions and without abiding— This is called the elimination of harm.
If one speaks of the various arhats, they are inconceivable to ordinary people;
their true nature is unchanging, and this cessation is called ultimate.
I formerly clung to the notion of a "monk," but having known it as it truly is, [I have abandoned it].
All phenomena are indestructible, yet they cause all beings to hear [the teaching].
To first grasp at a Tathāgata is called false;
knowing that there is no thought of difference, they are equal and one in emptiness.
To uproot and sever its very foundation is called the knowledge of non-arising;
if one can speak thus, one manifests the power of meditative concentration.
If one speaks of possessing all desires, such are the five names.
Able to be free from such conceptions, Like a phantom or a dream,
Neither increasing nor decreasing— This is called possessing the five desires;
Before the Savior of the World, He spoke thus.
Knowing that the nature of desire is empty, like the illusory forms in a dream,
one realizes that ultimately nothing arises and possesses the wisdom of suchness.
One knows that all errors and faults arise from false conceptualization.
By means of this ultimate wisdom, all things are fully perfected.
Being false and devoid of grasping, they are free from the characteristics of combination;
having thus understood them well, they are signless and non-existent.
With the same wisdom regarding all faults— whether wrong views or right views—
one attains the true Dharma, whereby both the characteristics of the false and the correct are extinguished.
The notions of birth and death among sentient beings are but the deluded discriminations of ignorance.
If one does not perceive sentient beings, then there is no birth and death.
Sentient beings employ many skillful means to abandon the notion of a life-span;
having distanced themselves from this notion, they realize that the notion of a life-span is the most evil.
If one is free from the notion of a sentient being, yet discriminates such things as a life-span;
to claim that one has taken the lives of many beings—this is what they have taught.
To abandon the notion of death is merely a discrimination of the deluded.
Ultimately attaining non-arising—this is called the true Dharma.
Having extinguished all fetters and proclivities, one realizes the signless;
awakening has no form, neither extinction nor fruit.
“Māra and his host cannot obstruct; one awakens to bodhi by oneself. All dharmas are free from dispute; their nature is unborn and quiescent.

When Mañjuśrī had spoken these verses, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of sentient beings were rid of all doubts and regrets. Having abandoned doubt and regret, their hearts were filled with joy, and they attained the illumination of the Dharma. Each removed their upper garment to offer it to Mañjuśrī, saying:

"May we all be able to attain this Dharma and speak it thus; may we also cause sentient beings to realize all dharmas within their own minds, so that they all attain the true reality (bhūtalakṣaṇa) as understood by Mañjuśrī."
At that time, Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

Why is it that these hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of sentient beings have all given rise to doubt and regret? For what reason does the Tathāgata not speak for himself to sever their doubts and regrets?”
Thereupon, the Buddha addressed Ānanda, saying:
"In this way, hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of sentient beings have all resolved their minds on bodhi under Mañjuśrī and have attained taming through Mañjuśrī."
Ānanda spoke again:
"Will they all attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?
The Buddha said:
"So it is, Ānanda! All sentient beings shall never regress from anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
"Why is this? It is entirely due to the spiritual friend Mañjuśrī. Ānanda said:

"Are all such bhikṣus—those who practice through faith, those who practice through the Dharma, srotāpannas, sakṛdāgāmins, anāgāmins, arhats, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas—completely free from the notion of being a śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha, and do they not fall back from anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?"
The Buddha said:
"There are those who find it difficult to believe, those of little wisdom and inferior capacity, those who are indolent, lazy, and lacking in diligence,
those who are greedily attached to food and drink and drawn to the five desires, and those who delight in the clamor of the crowd and do not distance their minds from it."
Those who have lost right mindfulness and lack wisdom; whose minds lack right concentration and are constantly agitated and distracted;
those who are conceited and cling to such conceit; those who are greedily attached to their own bodies, delighting in life and failing to contemplate impermanence;
those who are full of craving, envy, folly, and ignorance, and who violate the precepts with a mind of affliction.
They harbor malice and give rise to doubt and confusion regarding the Buddha-dharma; seeing those who lack wisdom, they associate with evil friends and distance themselves from virtuous friends;

relinquishing the notion of seeking karmic rewards, one should practice the Dharma-offering.
One who offers in this manner is said to perform the true offering.
To offer the Dharma as an offering is to honor the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body.

Even if one were to fill a hundred kalpas with offerings of clothing, bestowing many garments upon the World-Honored One, the Savior of the World; [it would not equal the merit of the Dharma-offering].
This is not called true worship; one who is able to uphold this sutra—this is called true worship, the most supreme and foremost.
Even if for a full hundred kalpas one were constantly to scatter all manner of celestial flowers;
To offer gifts to the various World-Honored Ones is not called true worship.
If one wishes to perform the foremost offering to the Saviors of the World who are able to deliver others, one should uphold this sutra; it can eliminate the marks of karmic retribution.

If one were to construct stupas of the seven precious gems for the sake of establishing the Savior of the World, making them all as vast as Mount Sumeru, this would not be called making an offering to the Buddha.
This [offering of the Dharma] is the greatest offering; it is the most supreme among all offerings.
One who is able to uphold this sutra does not perceive the marks of my physical body.
Even if one were to practice and maintain the prohibitive precepts for a full hundred kalpas,
yet fail to uphold this sutra, they cannot be called the most supreme.
Listening to the sutras while upholding the precepts is the highest form of upholding the precepts;
likewise, within the upholding of the sutras, one should have no thought of "upholding the sutras.
This is not called violating the precepts, nor is it breaking the precepts.
Those who are able to study this sūtra as I have explained it—
if they can study this sūtra, they are also well-versed in studying bodhi;
yet though they study bodhi in this way, in reality there is nothing to be studied.
One who can maintain the precepts in this manner, as revealed by this sutra, attains perfection in morality; such a person is called a keeper of the precepts.
Even if someone were to practice patience for a full hundred kalpas, [they would not equal one who maintains the precepts].
Though beaten and reviled, they do not retaliate; they are able to endure all things.
Even if their hands and feet are severed, they do not give rise to contrary thoughts;
nor do they harbor resentment or aversion, remaining free from all conceptualization.
One who can practice this patience fulfills it throughout a full hundred kalpas;
though they cultivate the patience of *rddhi*, their mind does not regard itself as superior.
This patience is the most foremost and is also called "well-cultivated."
If, moreover, one hears this sutra, Believes, understands, and upholds it,
This is called the most supreme patience, The foremost, beyond which there is nothing higher;
If, within this sutra, Having heard it, one is able to believe and understand.
Those who seek unimpeded, supreme Buddha-wisdom,
Should receive and uphold this sutra, And they shall swiftly attain it in its fullness.
Even if for a full hundred kalpas They were diligent and never sat down;
When the time for walking meditation has passed, one should dispel sleepiness.
The wise who cultivate this sutra should expound it for others;
thus they shall attain fearlessness—this is called supreme diligence.
Even if one were to attain the five supernormal powers after a full hundred kalpas,
if one has not heard this sutra, those powers are not called supreme.
If one can uphold this sutra, these are what are called supreme supernormal powers.
The supreme among supernormal powers is to know the meaning without attachment.
Even if one were to constantly act as a person of clear wisdom for a full hundred eons,
having accomplished worldly knowledge, one would still only have a definitive understanding of the world.
If one does not study this sutra, one cannot be called wise;
if one can uphold this sutra, one is then called brave and steadfast.
If one can understand it in this way, such a person is called wise.
One who upholds this sutra will, upon hearing it, be able to believe and understand it.
This sutra reveals the sphere of practice for the wise;
if one can uphold this sutra, they should apply themselves with even greater diligence and vigor.
At that time, Ānanda spoke again in verse:
"Even if one must travel a hundred yojanas, Or even a thousand yojanas;
One should go to where a wise person dwells, Where this Dharma of the sutra is found."
One should always go to where that [Dharma teacher] is, for the sake of hearing this sutra;
having heard it, one should believe and understand it, and one's mind should always remain in accord with it.
Even if the entire world were filled with fire extending for hundreds of thousands of billions of yojanas;
Wherever this sutra exists, the wise should listen to it with haste.
If one seeks the noble meditative absorptions— the most supreme among all dhyānas—
one should preach such a sutra as to extinguish all fetters and afflictions.
If there are those who wish to renounce and depart, yet remain attached to the world;
for their sake, this sutra is revealed as taught by the Buddha.
If one wishes to see all Buddhas, Akṣobhya is the most supreme.
Among all that is upheld, this sutra is the foremost.
Desiring to attain all happiness and to cultivate the practices of a bodhisattva, one should preach this sutra;
thus one will swiftly reach the place of peace and bliss.
"If you wish to see the Three Buddhas and the inconceivable Land of Peaceful Nurturing (Sukhāvatī),
you should expound this sutra just as the Buddha has taught it.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Ānanda:
“Excellent! Excellent!

When this sutra is being preached, if sons or daughters of noble family hear it, their minds will not be distracted; they shall read and recite this sutra, remain far removed from all places of worldly intimacy, and completely eliminate all perceptions and consciousnesses.”
If they wish to see the Buddha, they shall immediately behold him; at the time of their death, they will be able to face-to-face encounter hundreds of thousands of Buddhas. Why is this?

Because such sons of noble family are protected and remembered by all Buddhas; having heard this sutra, they further receive, uphold, read, recite, believe, and understand it, and also analyze and expound it for others.

Chapter Nine: The Land of Peaceful Nurturing (*An-yang-guo-pin*) The Sūtra of the Wheel of Non-retrogression, Chapter Nine: The Land of Peaceful Nurturing. At that time, from among the fourfold assembly of bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās, there was a young girl named Siṃhā (Lioness), who, together with five hundred other young girls, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
“If there is a woman who reads and recites this sutra, and further is able to analyze and explain it for others, how much merit will she obtain?
The Buddha told the girl Siṃhā:

“If there is a woman who dwells in *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and upholds, receives, reads, and recites such a sutra as this, and is able to speak of it for others, you should know that these are her final female bodies; she shall never again receive them.”

Why is this? Because they have already been able to receive, uphold, read, recite, and explain this sutra to others, their minds remain undisturbed, and all fetters and afflictions are completely extinguished.
"If this is a woman, any fetters that might arise should likewise be prevented from arising.
The Lion addressed the Buddha, saying,
"World-Honored One!"
"How is it that the marks of a woman can give rise to afflictions? The Buddha said, "Siṃha!"

If there is a woman who sees another woman of beautiful appearance, adorned with various necklaces, mani-jewels, and other ornaments, and experiencing such pleasure; having seen this, she immediately gives rise to defiled attachment and fails to practice discernment. She is like a painted vase that is merely decorated on the outside;
the vulgar and foolish are likewise foul and filthy, permeated by impurities and filled with excrement and urine, yet they do not know how to observe them.
Regarding such characteristics, she conceives a sense of delight and attachment, giving rise to a mind of passion. Because of these causes and conditions, she constantly receives a female body.

He further addressed Siṃha, saying: "All women are prone to much jealousy, deception, and falsehood; their hearts and mouths differ. Whether speaking face-to-face or for the sake of begging, they approach bhikṣus not for the sake of the Dharma, but with minds of anger or sloth and restlessness. They seek only clamor and intimacy with worldly affairs, thereby causing harm to this sutra. They are unwilling to listen, receive, explain, or recite it; day and night they constantly give rise to various afflictive states of mind, remaining far removed from liberation."
Because they possess such mental states as these, they receive a female body and cannot escape it.
Therefore, Siṃha! All women should conduct such an investigation as follows:
"How shall I sever all fetters and afflictions so that such unbeneficial matters as these women no longer occur?
One should listen to this sutra, receive and uphold it, read and recite it, and also explain it to others.
"Why is this? Because by hearing this sutra and discerning its sequential order, one will surely be able to abandon all fetters and afflictions. Then Siṃha said:
"If there is a woman who reads and recites this sutra and explains it to others, seeking to cast off her female body,
will she be able to attain it? The Buddha said, "Siṃha!"

If there are women who receive, uphold, read, and recite this sutra, this will be their final female body, and they shall never again receive one; except for those who intentionally manifest as women through the power of supernatural transformations.
"Siṃha! It is as if there were a person who lit a great mass of fire and threw himself into it; having already thrown himself into the fire, he further said:
'Do not burn my body, nor let my body take on a different color.'"
"Siṃha! What do you think? Although this person speaks these words, would they obtain what they have said?"
Siṃha replied, “No, World-Honored One.”
"Why is this? Because the nature of this great mass of fire is to burn things and extinguish bodily form.
The Buddha said:
"Siṃha! This sutra is also like this: it can burn away the firewood of all fetters and habitual tendencies.
If one wishes to cast off the marks of a woman's body, one will immediately attain freedom from desire and accomplish the Buddha-dharma."

Those who wish to see immeasurable, innumerable, and incalculable buddhas and attain unimpeded eloquence, and those who wish to give rise to a heart of loving-kindness toward all sentient beings, should likewise uphold, recite, read, and transcribe this sutra.
At that time, Siṃha and the five hundred maidens addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

From the presence of Dīpaṃkara Buddha, we heard this sutra and have upheld, recited, and studied it; we now, in turn, shall expound and reveal it once more for the sake of immeasurable sentient beings.”
At that time, Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
For what reason do this Lion and the five hundred young women not yet transform their female bodies?”
The Buddha asked Ānanda,
"Do you now consider these lions and five hundred maidens to be actual women? Ānanda replied:
"So it is, World-Honored One. Thus did the Buddha answer Ānanda.
"Do not speak such words. Why is this?
These lions and five hundred young maidens have all manifested in female forms; they are not real."
For what reason?

It is solely to manifest transformations for the sake of future sentient beings, out of compassion for all women, that he manifests in the form of a woman so that they may develop weary detachment from the female body.
Why is this? If one assumes a male form, one cannot enter all places. Ānanda!
These lions and others are neither male nor female.
Why is this? All dharmas are neither male nor female; they transcend all dharmas, and no characteristic can be apprehended—this is true illumination.
"Ānanda! These Lion and the others have taken on female bodies in accordance with worldly conventions, so as to transform all women by following their example in practice.
At that time, five hundred bhikṣuṇīs rose from their seats, prostrated themselves at his feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
From this day forward, we shall receive, uphold, read, recite, and transcribe this sutra, and explain it for others. Why is this? ”
"We have received this female body to no benefit; we should quickly cultivate weary detachment from it.

From this day forward, regarding that which we have not yet understood, we shall cause ourselves to understand it; regarding that which we have not yet heard, we shall cause ourselves to hear it. Throughout the first, middle, and last watches of the night, we shall eliminate sleep and maintain focused mindfulness and contemplation."
The Buddha said: "O bhikṣuṇīs! Excellent, excellent!"
"You all should adorn yourselves with the great adornment, rouse great diligence, and be foremost in valor; you must all cultivate weary detachment from and a desire to abandon this female body.
For the sake of benefiting all the Buddha-dharma, you should receive, uphold, transcribe, read, recite, and explain this sutra to others.
You all have now received this female body for the very last time."
When the bhikṣuṇīs heard these words, they leaped for joy and, all removing their upper robes, offered them as an act of worship to the Buddha.
Having made this offering, they spoke in verse:
"Having received your consolation, we shall obtain the body of a man."
"The Tathāgata speaks no double words; he is the supreme teacher among men.

At that time, within the fourfold assembly, there were five hundred wives of householders who rose from their seats, adjusted their robes, knelt with their right knees on the ground, joined their palms, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!

From this day forward, we too shall receive, uphold, read, recite, transcribe, and explain [this teaching]; yet, being constrained by our female bodies and lacking self-mastery, we must carry a fetus for ten months—how can we ever escape such suffering?

Why is this? Whether one is confined within the deep palace as a king, or restricted by parents, children, or sons-in-law, from this day forward, you should diligently apply yourselves with vigor, exclusively practicing and cultivating [the path], and uphold the True Dharma until the end of your lives.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One praised the five hundred wives of the elders:
"Excellent, excellent! It is as you have said.

From this day forward, you shall forever cast off the female body; you shall no longer be subject to serving others, nor shall you endure the suffering of ten months of pregnancy and the like. Free from lust and the various wombs, you shall be born constantly in pure Buddha-lands in every lifetime."
At that time, Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Where will these sisters be reborn after they have escaped their female bodies? To which pure land will they go?”
The Buddha said,
"These sisters shall be born in the world-system called Jewel-Treasury Lotus Light.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What is the name of the Buddha in that world?
The Buddha said:

"In that world there is a Buddha named Sarvaratnakāmadhvaja-prabha Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, who currently resides there, preaching the Dharma in various ways for the sake of all sentient beings."
"In this way, these daughters of noble family and others shall all be born in that land, and there, in the presence of that Buddha, they shall hear this sutra.

At that time, having heard the Buddha’s words, the elder’s wife was filled with joy and leaped for gladness; she immediately took off a necklace worth hundreds of thousands and scattered it over the Buddha as an offering.
Having made this offering, he immediately spoke these verses:
"We have received consolation, And shall abandon this female body.
The Tathāgata’s words are non-dual; All that he speaks is true."
The female body is most evil; may one vow to swiftly abandon it.
It is that which deludes the ignorant and foolish, who do not know its true nature.
The womb-born female is the most evil; may one vow never to receive such a body again.
"Once one has escaped the female womb, awakening shall be unsurpassed.
At that time, the wives of the elders gazed up at the Tathāgata, their eyes never wavering for a moment.
Śakra Devānām Indra scattered celestial māndārava flowers over the Buddha and said,
"We, too, shall receive and uphold this sutra.
The Buddha said:
“Kauśika! When you engage in battle with the asuras, may you always be victorious and never allow them to retreat or disperse.
At that time, Mañjuśrī, the Dharma Prince, together with hundreds of billions of sentient beings, all gave rise to the causes and conditions for wholesome roots.
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Even before the Tathāgata had resolved to attain bodhicitta, I had already turned this wheel of non-retrogression.”
The Buddha said: “Mañjuśrī!

In the ten directions, immeasurable billions of bodhisattvas all emit great, supreme radiance like the orb of the sun; likewise, this great earth also trembles in six ways, and the devas rain down flowers that fill and submerge the knees.”
At that time, Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
By what causes and conditions does the great earth tremble in six ways, and why do the devas rain down flowers?”
The Buddha said:
"These immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of devas, having heard what Mañjuśrī has spoken, have given rise to joy in their hearts; therefore, they rain down these flowers."
And they spoke these words:
"We shall all receive, uphold, copy, read, and recite this sutra; we also vow that we shall attain such a Dharma as Mañjuśrī has explained."
"Having heard this sutra, his heart was filled with joy; the entire great earth trembled everywhere, and the devas rained down flowers.
At that time, Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
This sutra can accomplish all great merits; this sutra is profoundly deep and most rare.
If there are sentient beings who hear this sutra even once, one should know that such persons have not come from small merit.
The Buddha said: "It is so, Ānanda!"

You should know that these sons and daughters of noble family have all already made offerings to the Buddhas of the past; for this reason, they are now able to hear this sutra within this assembly, give rise to faith and understanding, and are thus capable of receiving, upholding, reciting, and explaining it.
Wherever this sutra resides, that place is a stupa for all devas and humans; it brings immeasurable benefit, and its merit is not in vain.
As for the location where this scripture is kept, as well as those who can receive and uphold it, or even transcribe it, they should all be honored and regarded as the World-Honored One himself.

Those who hear this sutra will, at the end of their lives, all attain non-falling into the evil realms; they shall subdue all Māras, establish the banner of the Dharma, and constantly kindle the torch of the Dharma to illuminate all dark places. They shall be able to blow the conch of the Dharma to reach the Bodhi tree, beat the great Dharma drum to open and expound the gates of the Dharma, and rain down the great Dharma rain.
All those who seek the Dharma shall have their desires fully satisfied; they shall manifest the Dharma-realm and completely open the hidden treasures of all past Buddhas.

They shall know all phenomena, eliminating the notions of form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; they shall distance themselves from the notions of eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind, and remain free from all notions of phenomena, up to and including the notion of a Buddha.
Those who hear this sutra and believe, understand, accept, uphold, read, and recite it are true sons of the Buddha, all born from the Dharma. Ānanda!

If there are good men and others who wish to partake of the flavor of the Dharma and sit beneath the Bodhi tree at the site of enlightenment no different from me, they should all accept, uphold, read, and recite this sutra, explain it to others, and even carry its scrolls in their hands, honoring and making offerings to them with reverence.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
In the final age, will there be anyone who can receive, uphold, read, and recite this sutra, holding it in their hands with reverence and making offerings to it?”
The Buddha said:

"If you now hear this sutra and clearly believe, understand, and comprehend it, then in future lives you will also be able to receive, uphold, read, recite, and explain it for others, holding this sutra in your hands and paying it homage with offerings."
If there are śramaṇas, brahmins, devas, humans, or asuras who have now heard this sutra, it is impossible that they will not hear it again in future lives.
Why is this? Because by the power of the causal conditions of hearing the Dharma now, if one should hear the Dharma again in future lives, one will certainly be able to believe and understand it.

For example, suppose there is an elder who has many sons and daughters; his family is immensely wealthy with immeasurable treasures—gold, silver, lapis lazuli, coral, amber, musaragalva, agate, pearls, and conch shells; he possesses such things as male and female slaves, servants, elephants, horses, and carriages. Having placed all these treasures behind him, he travels to another region; when he returns to his original place, would he not recover these treasures?
Ānanda said: “I have. For what reason?”
"These treasures originally belonged to the deceased.
The Buddha said, "Ānanda!"
This Dharma-treasure, which you have now heard, is your own Dharma, which you shall hear again in the future.
With my Buddha-eye, I also see those in the present age who receive, uphold, read, and recite this sutra; they too shall later obtain it just as it is now, without any difference.
If there are sentient beings in future ages who receive and uphold this sutra, I shall observe them all with the Buddha-eye; they will be exactly as I see them now, without any difference.
"If there are those who slander this sutra, I see these people clearly with my Buddha-eye, just as I do today.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"If there are people who do not believe, do not understand, and instead slander this sutra,
where will they go? The Buddha said, "Stop!
Stop, Ānanda! Do not ask such a question.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I only pray that you will explain this.”
"May future sentient beings who lack faith, upon hearing of this retribution, become terrified and thereby give rise to faith and understanding.
The Buddha said,
"If one slanders [this teaching] and does not believe in its retribution, the suffering they undergo is equal in gravity to the five heinous crimes."
If one were to kill sentient beings with sharp blades until filling a trichiliocosm, what do you think—where would the retribution for that person's sin lead them?
Ānanda said, "The karmic retribution of this person shall lead them toward the evil realms.
The Buddha said:
“Ānanda! You should now understand it thus:

Suppose after the parinirvāṇa of as many Buddhas as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, someone were to construct stūpas and temples to make offerings to their śarīras, yet another person, with a malicious mind, were to burn and destroy them.”
"What do you think? How much retribution for their sins will these people receive?
Ānanda replied, "The suffering of the retribution received by such people as these would be so great that it could neither be described nor heard."
"If one slanders this sutra and speaks of its faults and evils, the retribution for the sin obtained will likewise be such that it cannot even be heard of. Why is this? "
"Because this person destroys the Dharma-eye of all Buddhas of the past, future, and present.
The Buddha said:

"If one sees someone who receives, maintains, reads, and recites this sutra, yet gives rise to slander, derision, and contempt, teaching others not to believe it and causing that person to be unable to read, recite, or receive and maintain it according to the Dharma, you should know that this person’s sin is extremely heavy and far greater than the former."

Ānanda said: "If all sentient beings filling a trichiliocosm were fully endowed with the ten wholesome paths of action and dwelling on the path to enlightenment, and if someone were to destroy the eyes of such persons, how much transgression would they incur?"
The Buddha said:
“For immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas, the bodies this person receives shall always be those of one born blind.
Within the hells, they shall undergo uninterrupted suffering, and their eyes shall be constantly gouged out.”
The Buddha said:
"If there is a person who gives rise to a mind of slander toward this sutra and does not believe it, I declare that the transgression of this person shall be equal to theirs."
Ānanda said: "If there are bodhisattvas who abide in awakening and, having faith and understanding in this sutra, receive, uphold, and do not doubt it, where will they go?
The Buddha said:
"This is called making offerings in accordance with all Buddhas, being no different from them. Ānanda said:
"If there should be someone who does not believe in this sutra and slanders it themselves, and also teaches others to give rise to such slander—"
"What kind of body will such a person receive?
What kind of suffering will they undergo?
The Buddha said:
"Stop! Stop, Ānanda!"
"Do not ask such a question. Ānanda said,

"I only pray that the World-Honored One will explain this at the proper time, so that if any among these four assemblies have doubts or give rise to lack of faith, upon hearing the Buddha's teaching, they shall repent their errors and gain faith."
The Buddha said:

"Furthermore, if there is a person who does not believe in this sutra and slanders it to others, they shall obtain a body ten thousand yojanas in height; receiving such a massive form, they will undergo immeasurable suffering."
Ānanda said, "Because this person was not careful with his tongue, what other characteristics does he have?
The Buddha said:
"The retribution for this person's sins is such that his tongue shall be one thousand yojanas in length and breadth;
five billion great, glowing-hot iron plows shall till his tongue, and five billion great, glowing-hot iron balls shall rain down upon it."
"Why is this? Because they did not guard against the transgression of slandering [the Dharma] through evil karma, they undergo such suffering.

At that time, having heard these words, the fourfold assembly’s body hair stood on end; with tears filling their eyes, they threw themselves upon the ground and, in a single voice, cried out these words:
“World-Honored One!

If sons or daughters of noble family should incur such sin by slandering [the Dharma] in this way, I now repent on their behalf so that their manifold sins may be extinguished, and they shall not undergo such great and evil retribution.”

Now, before the Buddha and before the infinite Buddhas of the other ten directions, we, being ignorant and deluded, did not recognize our own transgressions; yet the Buddha’s eye alone truly sees and truly realizes them, and we now repent for them all.

From this day forward, I dare not commit such acts again; like an infant who lacks understanding and cannot discern or comprehend the roots of goodness, I now offer my most sincere and profound self-reproach.
"I only pray that the World-Honored One will deign to show compassion and accept my repentance.
The Buddha said, "Excellent!"
"Excellent! At that time, the fourfold assembly each said:
"We now take refuge with a sincere heart; we confess all our transgressions and dare not conceal them."
The Buddha said,
"If you all repent with such sincerity, there are no wholesome dharmas that will not increase.
At that time, Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Are those who have now given rise to doubt within this assembly likewise possessed of the karmic obstacles of evil deeds?
The Buddha then replied:
"If anyone among this assembly should harbor doubts, they may immediately repent; all remaining offenses will result in only slight retribution.
Ānanda asked, "In what way will the retribution for their offenses be slight?"
The Buddha said:
"When such a person approaches the end of their life, they experience suffering within all their pores, which is no different from that of those in the hells."

Why is this? Because they are able to believe the teachings spoken by the Tathāgata, and they also believe in immeasurable asaṃkhyeya Buddhas, while likewise repenting of their own transgressions. Ānanda!

Those sons or daughters of noble family do not abandon the eye of all Buddhas of the past, future, and present; should they wish to see immeasurable asaṃkhyeya Buddhas, as well as the immeasurable, supremely wondrous marks of the golden vajra-leaf lotus light that shines everywhere.
At that time, Śakra-devānām-indra manifested in the form of an elder and scattered various kinds of flowers over the fourfold assembly, proclaiming these words:
"One should offer these flowers to the Buddha, and even offer them to such a sūtra as this."
At that time, the fourfold assembly took up the various flowers and scattered them over the Buddha; they transformed into a floral canopy, and they addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!

By what causes and conditions has this auspicious sign appeared? Why are there these lotus flowers now before the Buddha, and likewise such flowers before all the Buddhas as numerous as the sands of immeasurable Ganges Rivers?"
The Buddha said:
"It is because of the merit and power of expounding this sutra that these auspicious signs have appeared; you should know that such phenomena as these are all sustained by spiritual power."
At that time, Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Is it through the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power that the Dharma is protected and sustained to such an extent?”
The Buddha said, “Ānanda!
Truly, it is by my supernormal power that this Dharma is protected and sustained; even as many Buddhas as there are grains of sand in the Ganges all likewise protect and sustain it.”
At that time, Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What should this sutra be named?”
"How should this sutra be received and upheld?
The Buddha said:
"This sutra is named 'The Fruit of Non-Attachment'; it is free from all various mixed evil retributions. It should be received and upheld in this manner."

One should uphold this understanding that the faith-follower, the dharma-follower, the eight types of noble persons, the stream-enterer, the once-returner, the non-returner, the arhat, and the pratyekabuddha are all provisional designations and lack any ultimate reality.
It is called "Abandoning Māra"; thus should it be upheld.
It is also called "The Six Pāramitās"; thus should it be upheld. Why is this?

Ānanda! If there are good men or good women who possess such faith and understanding, who receive, uphold, read, recite, copy, and explain this sutra to others, you should know that these good men and good women are already fully endowed with the six pāramitās.
Ānanda asked: "How is it that by receiving, upholding, reading, reciting, copying, and explaining this sutra to others, one immediately becomes fully endowed with the six pāramitās?"
The Buddha said:
“If good sons and good daughters are able to have faith and understanding in this sutra, they are fully endowed with the dānapāramitā;
if their minds do not transgress the precepts regarding this Dharma, this is called being fully endowed with the śīlapāramitā.”
If one reads this sutra with a mind of patient endurance that does not regress, this is called being fully endowed with the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*);
if one’s mind does not sink back from this sutra, this is called being fully endowed with the perfection of vigor (*vīrya-pāramitā*);
if one has faith and delight in this sutra with a mind free from distraction, this is called being fully endowed with the perfection of meditation (*dhyāna-pāramitā*).
To thoroughly understand that this sutra is devoid of the characteristics of conceptual discrimination is called being fully endowed with the *prajñāpāramitā*.
Therefore, this sutra is in accord with the six *pāramitās*.
"It is also titled 'The Vast, Extensive, and Pure Wheel of Non-Retrogression Spoken by All Buddhas. Ānanda said,
"Even the name of this sutra cannot be heard, let alone seen."
"It is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end; it should be fully received and upheld.
The Buddha said: "So it is!"
"It is so! It is truly as you have said. Ānanda said:
“Having heard this sutra, how much longer will this person’s cycle of birth and death remain?
The Buddha said,
“If a person hears the name of the *Avaivartika-dharmacakra-vipula-vyūha-pariśuddha Vaipulya Sutra*, the remainder of this person’s birth and death will be but a thousand kalpas.”

Ānanda said: "If one hears the name of this sutra, believes and understands it, is able to receive it, and resolves to attain bodhicitta, in what stage should the merit of such a person be established?"
The Buddha said:
"If there are those who hear the name of this sutra, they shall receive the prediction of Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi and attain the stage of non-retrogression."
At that time, before the fourfold assembly, there appeared lotus seats of various colors, each with hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of petals.
Then the fourfold assembly leaped for joy and, taking these flowers, scattered them over the Buddha while saying:
"We shall all extensively expound such a sūtra as this for others, analyzing and revealing it so that it shall never be interrupted."
At that time, the World-Honored One smiled with serene joy; celestial music was played, and a fragrant breeze blew at intervals, its scent exquisite.
Many devas in the void likewise performed immeasurable varieties of celestial music and rained down celestial incense, fine powdered sandalwood, aloeswood resin, and Jāmbūnada gold dust.
Fine gold powder and various silver powders were spread over it, covered by nets of mani-jewel lattices,
as well as five-colored mandārava flowers, mahā-mandārava flowers, mañjūṣaka flowers,
mahā-mañjūṣaka flowers, karka-ra flowers, mahā-karka-ra flowers, and all kinds of utpala flowers.
Rohita flowers, kumuda flowers, and puṇḍarīka flowers, as well as fragrant garlands, ointments, and powdered incense—
all the offerings belonging to all the devas— filled the entirety of space.
The people on the ground likewise adjusted their robes and scattered flowers as an offering.

Furthermore, there were other sentient beings who all took off the precious bracelets from their arms and legs, the armlets, the various necklaces from their necks, and their immeasurable jeweled crowns, and presented them to the Buddha.
Furthermore, there were other sentient beings who scattered gold and silver over the Buddha.
Still others, their hearts filled with joy, raised a great sound and cried out: "Excellent!"

"Excellent! At that time, the elephants and horses emitted harmonious and elegant sounds, and the various birds in the void offered worship with calls appropriate to their own species. The sentient beings in the hells all attained temporary relief; the sentient beings among the animals came to regard one another with mutual affection, as if they were parents and children; all sentient beings in the realm of King Yama also experienced temporary happiness; and the sentient beings who were hungry ghosts were entirely freed from the suffering of hunger and thirst.

At that time, the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, non-humans, and others, each experienced happiness and felt mutual compassion for one another, just like fathers and sons.
At that time, Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
For what cause and condition does the Tathāgata now smile?"
At that time, the Buddha addressed Ānanda:

“All fourfold assemblies—bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās—as well as devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, non-humans, and others, who hear this sutra in this life or in future lives, shall all attain non-retrogression from anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.”
One who is able to expound this sutra extensively for others without any diminution is no different from my own current analytical exposition;
Ānanda, the very arising of faith and understanding upon hearing this sutra constitutes the seed of the Buddha, let alone its upholding, reciting, and practice.

You should know that for such a person, all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā) is not far off; they shall attain omniscience (sarvajñatā) and self-arisen wisdom (svayambhūjñāna). For this reason, this sutra is titled "The Seal of the Non-retrogressive Wheel of Dharma. It can bring great benefit to all bodhisattvas and serve as the causal condition for all sentient beings to resolve their minds upon the unsurpassed path.
Once they have been able to resolve their minds [on enlightenment], they will then fully accomplish this sutra. Ānanda!

The Tathāgata reveals this to all sentient beings through his omniscience: if there should be anyone who, though separated from the Buddha’s wisdom, merely hears this sutra, they will immediately attain natural wisdom (*svayambhū-jñāna*) and the wisdom of a Buddha, and will likewise receive a prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*). For this reason, this sutra is named "The Vast, Pure, and Adorned Wheel of Non-retrogression," and it is also named "The Accomplishment and Fulfillment of Wholesome Roots, Adorned with Skillful Means for Performing Beneficial Deeds for Those Who Practice the Mahāyāna."
"Ānanda, you should know!
At that time, as the Tathāgata extensively expounded this sutra, immeasurable bodhisattvas all attained the realization of the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*);
and immeasurable, boundless, incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) billions of sentient beings all came to abide in the stage of non-retrogression from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

When the Buddha had finished preaching this sutra, Mañjuśrī, Śāriputra, Ānanda, and the rest, along with the fourfold assembly of bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās, as well as devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans, were all filled with great joy. They received and upheld it with their heads bowed, paid homage, and departed.
